title: [Warmachine] Tabletop Battles Reviews: Cryx Dread Armada Models
content:
Yo ho, hi ho, it's a pirates un-life for me!

With the upcoming release of Dread Armada from SFG, we here at Tabletop Battles were lucky enough to get our hands on a set of preview models – these are STL’s designed to be 3D printed at home and used on the table.  We were provided with 5 different models: Blackbane, a solo, Gnara Drige, a second solo, Aiakos, a leader, one Ogrun Cannoneer, and finally the Heavy Warjack, the Deepstalker. In today's article, we will be going over our thoughts on these models, both in the quality and ease of their prints, as well as our experience painting these models and readying these models for glorious undeath.

I am going to avoid too much detail on the process of 3d printing itself, since there are numerous and better sources of information out on the internet (including some right here at TTB). Overall, the models printed well, though there were a few problems with Aiako’s supports. I suspect this will be fixed prior to the official release.

We would like to thank the Warmachine team for early access to these models for review.

Ogrun Cannoneer

The Ogrun Cannoneer printed beautifully.  I honestly have no negative feedback on this model. It's a wonderful level of detail without an overwhelming number of little greebles. I have only gotten a chance to half paint him, but I'm enjoying it immensely.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross

Photo Credit - Trish Ross

Gnara Dirge

The second model, Gnara Dirge also came out beautifully.  I printed her a total of 4 times, since I wanted to use her as the model I would test various schemes on.  The only downside I ran into with Gnara was that she was a bit delicate compared to the other Dread Armada models I printed. When I was removing supports her whip broke of right where it connects to her wrist on the first 2 prints.  So, be careful of that point you are removing supports in that area if you are printing her.

As for the quality of the sculpt, the detail on her face is wonderful.  This is one of the areas that 3d printing really blows old metal models from the olden days out of the water.  I have a giant pile of metal Styxis Blood Witches whose faces are abysmally cast metal blobs.  Every detail on Gnara, in comparison, is sharp and crisp.  An additional note; her whip is designed to contact and connect to the base, providing more strength to a part that is one of the most likely failure points.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Gnara

Aikos

Aiakos also printed wonderfully once the supports were adjusted (remember – preview copies may not be match the final retail release). He came in three parts: his body, his trident, and his base. I particularly like that the base itself was a totally separate part. As much as I love seeing Cryx showing their superiority over Menoth, it isn’t really my armies vibe, so when I paint the army up it will likely be replaced with rocks and waves.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross

Credit: Trish Ross

Carsor Blackmane

The final two models were the models I was MOST excited about.  First, Carsor Blackbane, Shadow of the Atramentous.  I know I’m not the only person who was excited to print him in transparent resin.  I also didn’t know what would work best, so I printed him twice in a standard resin, and 4 times with a transparent green resin (printer go brrrrrr).

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - What's better than 5 Blackbanes? 6!

The standard resin model came out cleanly with no problems. The transparent green resin also printed with no issues. The major difference in printing with the transparent green resin was I ensured every last support was removed before curing, and that they were 100% dry with no residual IPA on the model before curing.  The models came out wonderfully, and now I’m just trying to figure out how to make them even cooler.

The first model was a test model who ended up scrapped.  Such is the life of a Blackbane.

The second model was primed white, then painted with a coat of Army Painter Speed Paint Seafoam Green, then the flame bits were airbrushed black to create a dark flame effect.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross

With my 4 different transparent green models a few different experiments were done.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Clear Varnish Only

First, just a layer of gloss varnish. The goal here was to level out the surface imperfections and maximize the results, which can see the results for above.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Transparent Green with a white oil wash

Second I painted this model with a white oil wash, let it set, and removed the excess.  The original goal here was to accentuate the detail on otherwise transparent model.  Overall, while the results aren’t terrible, you really lose the transparent effect.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Clear varnish with black flames

For the third version, I simply airbrushed a few black flames over the fire to create some more depth.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Transparent Blackbane with Color Flames

The final version here is airbrushed flame.  Once it was printed in transparent green, then a base coat of white was airbrushed over the flame.  Once that was dry a later of yellow, orange, red, then finally black were added to the flames to create color.

Deepstalker

The final model to review was the Deepstalker.  This was actually the model I was most excited to get my hands on.  The detail is phenomenal and it really captures the feeling of the old Leviathan warjack.

My first question when I got ahold of the model was – does it mirror?  The answer is yes.  You can mirror the body STL without any trouble and the arms and heads still attach just fine.

Photo Credit: Trish Ross – Fred and is brother Derf.

The attachment style used for the arms is slightly different than we have seen in the past.  There is actually a small notch that limits the alignment of the arms, and I’m honestly not a huge fan of it.  It limits the locations of the arms which can already be a little finicky.  Removing it after the model has been printed will be a royal pain in the neck, so if you are planning on removing it, I would highly recommend removing the tab in whatever CAD software you have access to.

Deepstalker Body in Blender

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Deepstalker Body showing the arm alignment tab

The tab results in a weird little cutout on the arms that I suspect will be a future failure point.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Deepstalker Arm slot

My second criticism of the model is the heads.  While the model is beautiful, and shows a lot of character, the heads simply do not fit. I fiddled with it in person for a bit before opening the model up in blender and discovering the source of the problem. It looks like there's always going to be quite a bit of overlap unless the head options are updated.

Warmachine Deepstalker Head

My final criticism of the model is how far out the weapons reach.  Overhang has always been a problem in miniature games, and the Deepstalker is exceptionally bad.  The worst part – it’s the ranged weapons that have all the reach.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Deepstalker Overhang

While I have some criticism of the Deepstalker, I still love the model.  The detail wasn’t too fiddly, and I enjoyed painting it.  I put down a silver base coat with my airbrush, then did the remaining details with a brush and even with a simple scheme it looks sharp.

Photo Credit - Trish Ross - Deepstalker - I crave an oil wash!

Final Thoughts

I was super excited to get my hands on these models, and they did not disappoint.  I am certainly going to buy the tribe once it releases.  I had a few criticisms, but they are frankly mostly nitpicky details.   I also can’t wait to print and paint the tide tokens in transparent blue resin.

The Cryx player in me has missed playing a wall of Satyxis.  I always used to run max FA of them with Denny 1. I'm thrilled about the upcoming release and can’t wait for my printer to be running full time.

title: Marvel Crisis Protocol Tactics: Mirage, Havok, Jubilee & Multiple Man
content:
Mutants make up a large, popular corner of the Marvel Universe, so it makes sense that their various affiliations get plenty of releases in MCP. However, this one is particularly interesting, as the included models not only bolster the rosters of existing X-Teams but introduce two leaders for a brand new one - X-Factor! Covering a wide range of threats and gameplay niches, the Mirage, Havok, Jubilee & Multiple Man box brings an exciting next chapter for MCP’s mutants.

Havok

Image Courtesy AMG

Havok opens the box as a 4-Threat brawler who isn’t terribly flashy (ironic, given his power set) but can do solid damage and apply helpful conditions from afar. His stat line is pretty spot-on for the average 4-Threat in the post-August-errata world, maybe even a bit under, with only 6 HP on his injured side. It’s never great when a character has Physical as their lowest defensive stat, given that it’s the most common attack type in the game (and used for dodging), and without any defensive tech, Havok isn't a guy who wants to take too many hits.

At first glance, his two attacks also seem fairly milquetoast. Range 4, 5 dice with a wild incinerate trigger for Plasma Blast is perfectly reasonable without being overly exciting, and a B4, 7-dice Plasma Wave with Pierce on a wild and auto-Incinerate is quite nice, but 5 power is a lot! Fortunately, Havok has two ways to help those attacks hit a little harder. Plasma Dispersion is an innate power that lets Havok modify a die to a Hit for every Wild he rolls. It’s dicey, but he has a 52% chance to hit the Wild on 5 dice and 65% on 7.

His other boost to output (and survivability, if needed) is his leadership, Government Sanctioned, which should look familiar. It’s a lot of text, but it’s functionally the same as Star-Lord’s Winging It tokens. Hand one out to three characters in the Power Phase, and spend them to get two rerolls when attacking or defending. However, unlike Star-Lord, Havok requires either the attacker or defender to be contesting or holding a Secure/Extract. It also can’t be used on dodge.

Will there be niche cases when neither the attacker nor defender is on/with a point, or you wish you had it for dodge? Sure, but functionally, it’ll be the same as Winging It more often than not. Fortunately, Winging It is quite good! I don’t think Government Sanctioned is the best leadership in the box, but it seems perfectly reasonable for a punchier flex when Multiple Man doesn’t seem like the right call. He’s also affiliated with the X-Men.

Overall, Havok seems like he’ll be a perfectly fine affiliated dude, and he comes with two TTCs. Mutant X is unaffiliated and lets Havok pay 5 to play himself within Range 5 and grant an ally a superpower to heal 1 damage the first time it deals damage during its activation. It’s a neat effect, but it’s realistically not going to add up to too much healing. The Range 5 place might be worth it, but 5 Power is a lot, and he drops any Objectives he’s holding.

Tactical Operation is likely better. It’s an X-Factor Affiliated card that lets Havok pay 1 Power to let an X-Factor character Advance Short and interact after an enemy is Dazed/KOed. The obvious use is to pick up an Extract that was just dropped, but you can also use it to interact with a Pay to Flip, or simply move over to a Secure or into range to attack.

Multiple Man

Images Courtesy AMG

If Havok is too straightforward, Multiple Man makes up for it with a complex, flexible kit and an exciting leadership. Jamie Madrox starts off looking pretty underwhelming, with an under-par 4-3-3 defensive line and only 13 total health at 4 threat. A range 2, 5-dice Strike also doesn’t inspire confidence, nor does a 3-cost, 7-dice Madrox Monkey Pile. Fortunately, Multiple Man has plenty of tricks up his sleeve to get more mileage out of those numbers and impact wide swaths of the board with scenario presence. If Multiple Man’s Duplicates are within 2 of the defender for either attack, Jamie gets to reroll 2 (builder) or add 2 (spender) dice to the attack, putting him up there with the hardest-hitting 4 threats.

But the grunts aren’t just dice boost bots. The grunts have a standard 4-dice Grunt attack, but they can reroll 2 dice if Multiple Man is within 2 of the defender, which is very high damage potential for a Grunt. Moreover, these Grunts can apply Slow with the attack and interact with all objective types. They need an allied character also contesting to score, but that’s still huge. But wait, there’s more! Jamie can pay two power for Duplicate Reabsorption, which moves an Extract from the Grunts to Multiple Man, KOs the Grunts, and heals Jamie a whopping three damage (RIP Sandman).

The Grunts pop out whenever Multiple Man takes damage, and they don’t come out Staggered. With a self-throw (Follow the Leads) that damages Multiple Man (and whoever he funs into), he can easily get the Grunts out.

Multiple Man also packs the second X-Factor leadership, and it’s a doozy. X-Factor Investigations not only gives allies an extra power in the power phase if they’re contesting a Secure, but it also lets any allied character reroll one die when interacting with an objective. This obvious synergy is Pay to Flips, but it also works on things like Skrulls and any future Extracts that require rolls. With leadership and Grunts that can Interact, Multiple Man seems like a powerhouse scenario leader who can also put out massive damage if his Grunts are nearby. Jamie is also affiliated with the Uncanny X-Men.

Multiple Man gets access to two TTCs in this box. Dangerous Business is somewhat similar to Warpath, letting Jamie pay 1 Power after an allied X-Factor character is attacked (before damage is dealt) to let them Advance Short. It’s cheap, and the effect is strong, so I expect it to see regular play in X-Factor. Multitasking also seems great. For no Power cost, Jamie can play the card to remove the superpower from his Grunts that requires another ally nearby to interact or provide context. Big scoring potential there.

Mirage

Image Courtesy AMG

Mirage is a 3 Threat with incredibly high potential, but hoops you have to jump through keep it in check. She’s got a perfectly average 3-threat stat line, but she’s one of very few in that band with a range 5 builder (Neurokinetic Arrows). One a wild, her arrows give the defender a Neural Connection token, which turns on other parts of her arsenal. Psionic Salvo is a perfectly good Spender at 7 dice with a two-die trigger to make the same attack into a different character.

If enemies have a Neural Connection token, Mirage can spend 2 Power to Advance them short (at Range 5!) with Figment of Fantasy. She can also force attackers within 1 to reroll 2 attack dice, but that range goes up to 5 if they have a Neural Connection token. Time will tell how easy it is for her to drop these tokens where she wants (and she can only have one out at a time), but the effects are very strong for her threat.

Mirage also packs a New Mutants leadership, Coming of Age. It’s a unique effect that grants allies 3 Power and a Self Discovery Token when they flip to their injured side; they can spend the latter to add three dice to a defense or dodge roll. Mirage is also affiliated with X-Force and SHIELD.

Mirage has one TTC, Confront the Demon Bear. For 2 Power and an action, Mirage can make a Range 5, 7-dice attack and give the target a Neural Connection token. It’s not the most impressive card, since her main attack is already range 5, but it helps when you can’t risk needing to roll a Wild to hand out her token.

Jubilee

Image Courtesy AMG

The last character is Jubilee, who is instantly interesting for being one of the game’s few 2-Threat characters. She’s a 2-2-3 with 4 HP on each side, and she’s got a seemingly now-standard 2-Threat drawback on her scoring potential.

Lumikinetic Blast is a solid gainer, throwing 4 dice at range 4 with a Wild/Hit Stun trigger. She’s likely to be perfectly happy occasionally sitting on a back Secure and fishing for those annoying early-game Stuns on the opponent’s centerpiece model. Princess of Pyrotechnics is a 6-dice spender at range 3 with the same Wild/Hit trigger for rapid fire. Not too shabby.

Jubilee also has two Reactive Superpowers that help her stay alive and/or support her team. Fireworks lets her buy defensive rerolls for herself or allies within 2, and Wolverine! thematically lets her redirect an attack from herself to an allied James Logan Howlett within range 2.

But there’s a downside. I Totally Meant to Do That! forces Jubilee to drop any objective tokens she’s holding whenever she rolls a Crit, but he also gets a Power for her trouble. She’ll be fine sitting on a Secure, especially if Logan is nearby, but picking up an Extract is risky business. She’s mono-affiliated in X-Men, and time will tell if they need her help with threat math and which leader(s) want what’s in her toolbox.

Jubilee also gets two TTCs in the box. Blood Cursed doesn’t seem overly strong, but it’s thematic and fun. She can play the card for free during deployment, and it grants her a Reactive Superpower. After being attacked, she can pay 3 Power to place it next to her attacker, roll some dice, and deal/heal for every Crit and Wild. Though it’s hard to imagine her surviving too many hits with her defenses and HP.

Light Up the Sky lets her reroll one attack die every time an enemy attacks from within Range 3 of her. It’s a solid support effect for only 2 Power that could make its way into Rosters/Squads with more limited options.

Lastly, this box also comes with a non-character-specific X-Force card called Covert Operations. If it looks familiar to the soon-to-rotate Pretty Sneaky, Sis, that’s because it is! That card lets X-Force characters pay 2 Power to require attackers to be within Range 2 to target them. Now, an X-Force leader has to pay all the Power, but it also works on unaffiliated splashes.

Overall, the Mirage, Havok, Jubilee & Multiple Man box is a bit of a mixed bag. I’m not overly sold on Havok, and Jubilee remains a question mark with potentially high highs but some important drawbacks. Mirage seems like a slam dunk for her affiliations, and Multiple Man hits the perfect balance of creative and powerful.

title: Mayday, Miss Marcy! Making the Worst of a Bad Situation
content:
Welcome back once again to Mayday, Miss Marcy!, our weekly advice column where readers submit their burning questions and I quaff them with cool, tempered advice. Or something. Not my best intro. Anyway! Welcome back everyone and as we approach the middle of October, we've got another batch of spooky questions (in that it makes me shiver thinking about some of these situations at times) ready for your perusal on this fine Thursday. If you're curious how to get your own questions answered in this very column, please read the blurb below:

Have a question you want answered on just about anything you’d need advice on in this grand hobby space of ours? Board games, 40k, AOS, TTRPGs, MTG, anything and everything that we cover, we can help with!

For some examples, take a look at previous editions of our column at this link with a handy tag to see all previous questions and answers!

If you want to submit questions, we have a few ways you can do it. Patrons can use the Discord bot command to ask questions, which will be received anonymously!

If you’re not a Patron, or just don’t want extra steps, you can comment on this article, or e-mail me directly at marcy@tabletopbattles.com!

Last week, we tried to help out someone learn that is isn't easy being green, especially when you want to be yellow, as well as two other questions. This week, we've got another selection of questions, so let us get right down to it!

What's The Worst That Could Happen?

Marcy,

At a recent LGS run tournament, it was discovered that a player was cheating by using loaded dice. The store promised to take appropriate action, distribute the prizes by discounting the player, and it seemed as though things would be fine. However, the player has disputed that they were cheating and have continued to come to the store to argue, to the point that they were recently trespassed. This has now spread further, and the end result has been that players have been leaving the LGS, making it hard to even get regular amounts of games for events.

I'm honestly just confused and pretty pissed off at this because my store is now essentially dying for doing the right thing, which is to punish a cheater, and yet we're all suffering for it. I don't run the store or really know the staff or owner that well, but it is my local store, and the next one I could play at is a considerable drive. I don't even really know what to do, if anything.

Cheated Out of Games

Dear Cheated,

I think the best thing I can probably suggest here is that you just need to ride out whatever is happening. This sadly sounds like small-town interpersonal beef, and that stuff can get really nasty when people make things exceptionally personal. Obviously the cheater sucks, and it isn't really fair that the store owner / environment is suffering, but it makes me think that there is a lot of effort being pushed to punish the store for exposing a cheater (such as social media posts, etc.) that are driving people away because they just don't want to be involved in any capacity.

If you are committed because this is your local shop and you really don't have anywhere else to go, then what you need to do is protect your own interests. And by that, I mean that you should obviously stay out of whatever fight is happening, but also you should try to more strongly push for people to play and come to the store. The drama will inevitably die down because either something will happen to cause it to end or it will simply burn out, but players leaving means that things must be pretty bad or the vibes are weird or something. If you and a few other players can put in some coordinated effort to ensure there's always people willing to play, and building a community of players, you can likely help; and if not, maybe making better connections with the players in the store can help you find alternatives to pursue.

Bad Reputation

Miss Marcy,

I have developed something of a bad reputation. I used to get angry and generally was pretty unpleasant to be around. Sadly, a lot of that turned out to be due to being undiagnosed and some other personal issues, and now that I've made some changes and improved things, I'm finding that it is really hard to escape that reputation. Is there really nothing I can do? People aren't obligated to forgive, interact, or correct how they feel, but it does feel kind of bad that factors I couldn't control that are now controlled are still negatively impacting me.

Beautiful Princess Disease Haver

Dear BPD,

I appreciate you putting what it is exactly that was the problem in the reply, even as a joke for your name; I think that it also sheds some light on the issue. I'm not sure exactly what the timespan is here, but it sounds like the change might still be fairly recent in people's minds. The mindful statement you make is also sadly the albatross: people are going to have to really work to get over the preconceived notions they have about you, because their first and majority interactions were when you were undiagnosed and not being able to make changes. Even if you explain it to those people now, they aren't your friends or family, it sounds like they are local players at a shop; they don't really owe you anything, and you really shouldn't also have to constantly go 'hi, I have BPD, I am now getting treatment,' to every single person. I think the sad answer is people are also just allowed to dislike other people, and your first impressions may not have done much to help you there.

That said, I want to be hopeful and say that I think you just need to give it more time, both for the people you're interacting with and yourself. A part of this equation I'd think of after reading your question is are these people you WANT to be around, or do you now feel a sense of guilt or obligation to show them that you weren't really that person from before? Because if it is the latter, it may just be better to move on to another store or place to frequent; if you have no big lingering attachment, I'd suggest trying a new place and a new start for yourself. Congrats on getting things sorted out, also.

From the Ashes

Hi Miss Marcy,

Recently, my partner's family suffered a pretty catastrophic loss from a fire, which ended up destroying their collection of models. Thankfully no one was hurt and all of the family and pets are safe, but I have noticed that my partner seems pretty depressed about the things they've lost, and I'm unsure of exactly how to help in this regard. I've talked, or at least circled, that they should consider getting a new set of models and that I'd be happy to help them restart, but they seem a little resistant to the idea in general. I can't tell if it is recency, disinterest, or not wanting to re-invest in something after having lost it. If they do want to move on then that's fine, but my gut tells me they're more worried about money and time.

Wanting to Help

Dear Wanting,

That is kind of a tough one. I can certainly sympathize with the idea that the loss of the models and other things is still recent and thus hasn't fully sunk in, but I'd also wonder if maybe they're feeling reluctant because having lost what they had makes the fear of getting new things you could once again lose at a moment's notice less appealing. There could even be storage or cost issues as you mention, and I don't really know if I can offer you an answer, because I don't really know your full situation. I would probably say that the biggest thing you could do and suggest is simply continue supporting them; there are likely a lot of really complex feelings going on with what's happened, and even just the thought that my partner would want me to continue my hobby and pursue my interests would at least be something I'd enjoy knowing. Even if your partner decides to move on to something else, the fact that you want to support them is what matters. If it does seem like the want to and are worried about cost, consider helping them find second hand models on social media or marketplace listings that are local; the volume you can get there can sometimes help offset some of the cost, especially since a lot of it might be built.

title: Kill Team: Crafting a Custom Killzone
content:
For the last few weeks here at Tabletop Battles, we’ve talked a lot about how to win while playing Kill Team, but just how do you have fun while playing Kill Team? In this article, we’re going to lean more into the storytelling and narrative aspect of things and how you can use the books, models, and terrain features you already own to craft exciting stories with your operatives. First up is crafting a custom Killzone!

Deathwatch breaches the base of a Tomb Pyramid that has emerged in the midst of the city.

Terrain Features

While Approved Ops gives us an excellent framework for organizing and playing at competitive events, after nearly a year of playing the same maps, the novelty can wear off. Many times players will go up to their assigned table and go “Oh, this map.” Creating a custom Killzone is one of the easiest ways to inject new life into your games and keep things feeling fresh, especially if your local community is feeling a bit burnt out playing the same six layouts from Approved Ops.  

The easiest way to do this with a Killzone like Volkus or Octarius is to simply separate the pieces by type and give half of them to each player, perhaps rolling off for a unique piece like the Octarius Oil Pump or Volkus Rubble Pile, if not excluding them all together. Players can then alternate placing a terrain feature to create a weird and whacky Killzone that’s never been seen before or since. 

Throwing new pieces into the mix can be a way to spice up your tabletop room nights. Expansions like Typhon, and Blood and Zeal added new terrain features to use for Volkus, and they’re a fun way to add some visual variety to the usual ruins and rubble you find on that Killzone, but they work perfectly well Octarius, and even within the confines of a Tomb World or the corridors of Gallowdark. Tyranid infestation can easily begin to subsume the Necron design. Imperial defenders might rally to protect a shrine in their cathedral ships. Even if you don’t have these particular pieces, you can still use other objects to take their place; from other terrain pieces you might own to the Poorhammer classic, the humble coke can. Don’t let a little thing like a lack of plastic stifle your creativity in these endeavors.

Alien growth overruns also alien ruins.

The Mission

You’ve got your terrain, but just what are your operatives trying to accomplish? Breaking away from the Approved Ops format can give you the opportunity to experience a more lore centered approach to the game. If you’ve been to a narrative event, whether that’s at Games Workshop's own Regional Opens or just one hosted at your FLGS, you’ve probably seen how exciting these can be. 

Mission markers can be placed underneath things like the Tyranid gestation sacs or spore chimneys to simulate planting explosives at these sights and clearing them out. If you're using Necron Tomb World pieces, operatives might need to place scanning devices next to those pieces and then prevent the encroaching metallic skeletons from destroying them. Finally, you may decide to just use the Nemesis Operatives book and forgo a traditional mission entirely, instead making the objective to destroy an entrenched enemy artillery position or a Land Raider that blocks the path of a main army's advancement. 

The Kill Team Core Book has some good map layouts with markers preplaced as well as suggestions for how to place them yourself, so looking at those can give you a better understanding of where objectives should go. Don’t feel beholden to these though, and you can even utilize fewer or more objective markers if you think the mission becomes more interesting if you do so. We also suggest you place markers before terrain, that way players have some agency in where their terrain is placed relative to those spaces. Depending on the mission you’re playing you may not even have to set up objective markers; if your mission is simply “Kill the Nemesis Operative”, a desperate last stand against an enemy onslaught, or a retreat from one side of the Killzone to the other, objective markers are irrelevant to glory.

XV26 Stealthsuits defend against a cadre of Chaos Raptors in an NPO game.

Unique Killzone Rules

So now that you’ve made your pieces for the Killzone, what are the next steps? For some, just creating this fresh new environment will offer a novelty to keep you satisfied until new Approved Ops drop, but what if you want even more? Adding unique Killzone rules is a way to further create fun narrative sequences, even if you aren’t playing within a narrative framework. 

Games Workshop themselves have several rules pages dedicated to this endeavor. In Killzone Volkus, you have The Great Gun Fires, which gives you rules for the firing of the vaunted Massif Ballistus. Once you try out that mission, you see the possibility that begins to unfurl. Perhaps your homebrew Killzone is suffering from dust storms, making any shooting outside 6” Obscured. If you’ve added Tomb World walls to your Killzone, alien energies can discharge into operatives who Reposition too closely to them, dealing minor damage. Bheta Decima gantries have their own rules that work well to create cramped industrial sectors with crates and cranes. 

If you’re struggling to come up with some things, the Kill Team App has the Ctesiphus Expedition Campaign rules in the mission packs tab. From pages 13-16, there are various “conditions” for Tomb World and Volkus that have exciting changes to them. You can roll a dice for them for a random surprise or just decide with your friend which one sounds the most fun.

If you are deciding to play within a narrative framework, whether that’s with Ctesiphus Expedition or your own custom one, you can also create effects that roll over from mission to mission or are consequences/bonuses from previous missions you succeeded in. Securing munitions in one mission could give you a free Ammo Cache equipment in subsequent ones, or perhaps you were stealing medical supplies from an enemy camp to gain a once per game Heal of some sort. Creating a narrative framework can be a fun way to create some consistency and rewards for your games of Kill Team.

Organizing the Killzone

With the rules and terrain pieces decided on, the final step is actually organizing all this into a cohesive battleground. By design, this article is not a framework for creating balanced Killzone environments, nor do we recommend it be used as such. Nevertheless, to craft an experience that’s enjoyable for both players, a few basic rules should be followed. Make sure deployment zones have sufficient Heavy terrain to provide initial staging for operatives. While symmetrical Killzones are very easy to do and create an innately balanced experience, they can also cheapen that first initiative roll; if the sides are the same, the winner has no incentive to pick a side and should just take a reroll card. So throw a little asymmetry into the mix to create some tactical decision making. If you’re playing a regular game with objective markers, make sure they’re spread out in a way that’s fair as well.

Of consideration is the mission itself. If you’re playing some sort of custom escort mission or Nemesis Operatives make sure there’s enough space for larger models to move relatively unhindered. If you’re playing a last stand or mission where you need to go somewhere specifically in the Killzone, placing the strongholds next to each other can provide a strong defensive position to either assault and destroy, or die gloriously within. Kill Team is by its nature a cramped game, so deciding ahead of time what your mission is lets you organize a Killzone appropriately. 

Bringing It All Together

So now that we’ve given you a framework to operate within, let’s see how it plays out in the real world. I’ve created a custom mission and killzone using these rules, and we’ll walk it step by step. Firstly we decide on a Killzone. I’ve chosen Volkus, and Tyranid fan boy that I am, we’ll be using the larger terrain features combined with Tyranid terrain features from Kill Team: Typhon. 

Our custom Killzone. Note we've utilized five objective markers instead of three.

Playing a "traditional" game of Kill Team, we’ve decided to utilize the elite hunters of the Xenos Deathwatch on their mission to infiltrate an infested portion of a city under siege. The Deathwatch mission is simple; destroy the spore chimneys and gestation sacs populating the sector. They do so by moving with 1” of these terrain features and performing a 1AP mission action: Plant Charge. At the end of the game, Deathwatch receives a victory point for each objective they’ve performed Plant Charge on, and a bonus point if they perform it on all five of them. 

The Hive Mind will organize a response to these invaders however. A Kill Team of Raveners defends this critical infrastructure and will do everything in their power to slow down the Deathwatch before Tyranid reinforcements arrive and overwhelm the strike team. The Raveners will receive a victory point for each objective successfully defended, and a bonus point if they defend more than the Deathwatch destroyed. 

My opponent and I also decided that while we would play with Kill Op to create a secondary victory condition, that playing with the Tac Op would distract from the mission at hand for both sides, so we’ve omitted that facet. We’ve also decided Tyranid spores are heavy in this sector, and so both sides will be obscured if performing a Shoot more than 6” away, though you can very easily say the Tyranids have evolved to see through this miasma if you decide to. 

After that we decide which side of the board both sides begin on, and the game begins in earnest. With the creation framework we’ve provided here, you can very easily recreate this mission, or any number of other ones, battle it out yourself to see whether the Tyranids will defend their brood, or if Deathwatch will suffer not the alien to live! 

Final Thoughts 

With many players being die-hard competition junkies, myself included, it can be easy to forget that Kill Team gives us an excellent system to simulate those movie and game moments we all love so much. Casual Kill Team games give us the opportunity to create some of those movie moments ourselves, and do the thing we all like to do: smash our models together and make them fight to the death. We hope this article has given you some good ideas for how to play the game outside of these competitive environments, and have some good old fashioned fun.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don't forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website, and subscriber-only content covering competitive Warhammer 40K!

Welcome to Competitive Innovations, our serialized feature for a number of game lines across the tabletop wargame space. Our army list and tactics experts canvass the top tournaments for their game of specialty, looking at the month’s top match-ups and how they played out on the tabletop to let you know what’s hot, what’s not, and what might be coming next as the competitive meta evolves year-round.

Another month of GTs has passed, and with it, more players are finding the best ways to bring their favorite armies to the top. With September also being the month of LVO we have decided to make a separate article covering LVO since it deserves its own coverage for Star Wars Legion. Do we have any big meta shakeups this month? Are we still in the era of the Tauntaun brothers dominance? Let's get to the stats and find out.

Thoughts

This Rebel list has a lot of the usual suspects aside from a lightsaber-wielding, Tauntaun-riding commander of the Echo Base forces. Sniper teams and Commandos have proven to be more than worth their weight in points and activations, forcing characters or other more difficult to kill units to be properly positioned lest they take some unblockable damage, or even need to roll dice against multiple crits. Hantaun is a wrecking ball of a unit that has helped define the current Rebel list building, and it is clear with this list that he is here to stay. A unique inclusion is Operative Luke, who on his own is a powerhouse of a unit with the ability to jump from melee to melee with Disengage on his unit card, a rarity in Star Wars Legion. A tanky unit with a massive 4 courage with a suite of command cards that can control the battlefield around him, it is no wonder Brian Bear has been singing Operative Luke's praises for a while now. Triple ATRT with the Rotary Blasters brings some fast and efficient Anti-Armor to round out the list.

5th - Rob Mowgly Rowland - A 20 activation Empire list running Thrawn/Krennic and maxing out on Shoretroopers and Mortar Troopers.

6th - Brian LevityGames Labay - LevityGames - An empire list headed by Iden and Krennic with Operative Vader and 3 strike teams but no snipers, just the Sonic Charges.

7th - Daniel Avalos - An Ashoka and Yoda list with triple arcs and ATRT's for some anti-infantry and anti-armor.

8th - Isaac Pendley - A Rebel list with the Hauntaun brothers tripe snipers and ATRT's and Cassian fleet troops. A group of all the best Rebels have to offer.

Congratulations to all players who were able to make it and the top 8 for 3 long days of Star Wars Legion rounds. You all did a fantastic job!

A GAR list that brings Yoda and Padme for some token support as well as Yodas entire kit. title: Trench Crusade reveals medical crowdfunder for Warhammer art legend Karl Kopinski
content:
The team at Factory Fortress Inc, makers of Trench Crusade, have announced a new fundraising campaign to support Karl Kopinski, a prolific fantasy artist best known for his work on Warhammer 40,000 and Warhammer Fantasy Battle in the early 2000s, and who is still recovering from a stroke he had in 2025. Hosted on 3D model marketplace MyMinifactory, 24 model creators including "top wargaming brands" will contribute "high quality STL packs" to a bundle of digital miniatures that will be available on November 5.

Kopinski suffers from the blood disease myeloma, and has been receiving treatment since 2019. In March 2025 he suffered a stroke as a side-effect of regular treatment, which left his left side numb and paralyzed, and he is still recovering to this day.

Wargamers and fans of Kopinski's artwork rallied around him with a Gofundme campaign to pay for living expenses for him and his family while he was unable to work. This raised $73,000 dollars in just four days, and at the time of writing, the total is now $142,000.

Kopinski was a full-time artist in the Warhammer design studio from from 1998 to 2005, where he was a major contributor to the tone of Warhammer 40k third and fourth edition, and Warhammer Fantasy Battle sixth edition. His work on Codex covers is timeless - Abaddon grasping Cadia in the Talon of Horus is particularly iconic.

As a freelancer, Kopinski has worked on many properties, including plenty of MTG sets for Magic: the Gathering. He even made the art for the Timmy, Power Gamer card, which you may have seen as a player avatar on MTG Arena.

Writing in the Trench Crusade Facebook group, the game's lead designer Tuomas Pirinen says "Karl is my friend as well as my housemate during my GW days, so I am so glad we can help him and his family". Factory Fortress' main role in this campaign has been organizing other creators, but there will be a brand new digital miniature for the game included in the reward bundle.

If you want to back the campaign when it opens, you can follow it now on MyMiniFactory.

Myeloma, often called 'Multiple Myeloma', is a form of blood cancer originating in the bone marrow, which causes the body to produce abnormal plasma cells. Ordinary plasma cells fight infection by producing antibodies, but cancerous cells produce useless 'paraproteins' instead. The cells and paraproteins build up in the blood, crowding out functional cells. According to the American Cancer society, the disease affects about one in 108 men and one in 133 women.

If you're a fan of Kopinski's work, come and share your favorite pieces in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: Wizards of the Coast rejects D&D union effort, says it's "not neutral"
content:
Wizards of the Coast "doesn't intend to voluntarily recognize the D&D or Studio X" teams' efforts to join the United Wizards of the Coast Union, according to a statement made on the Union's X dot com account on Wednesday, October 14, and confirmed by a spokesperson for WotC. The matter will now be referred to the National Labor Relations Board, leading to a secret ballot in which all staff will vote to decide whether or not to adopt the union.

Staff in the Dungeons and Dragons team and Studio X - the catch-all group that includes most creative staff working on Magic: the Gathering - announced their intention to join United Wizards of the Coast (UWOTC-CWA), part of the Communication Workers of America union, on October 6.

UWOTC-CWA formed in June this year, and was founded by members of the Magic the Gathering: Arena development team. Wizards of the Coast chose not to voluntarily recognize that union, leading to a vote which passed with a landslide 83% of workers in favor.

UWOTC-CWA is campaigning for unionization on the following platform:

  • "Fair wages, career progression, and job security: Workers should be secure in the face of industry instability, roles should be clearly defined, and workers should be able to grow their careers through meaningful raises, role changes, and promotions.
  • Remote work protections and sustainable workloads: We have been asked to do more work with less regard for our personal lives. Intensive crunch and forced RTO aren't just bad for business. They hurt workers' families and communities, which in turn affects the work we can produce.
  • Reliable and easily accessible healthcare: Wizards of the Coast workers and families should not have to worry about the quality of their healthcare. We wish to decrease the bureaucratic red tape around healthcare claims and provide reasonable deductibles and co-pays to our members.
  • Protection against the encroachment of AI: Leadership, without regard for the desires of our teams, has pushed for adoption of LLMs and generative AI. This has to stop; our teams deserve a robust and enforceable AI policy that aligns with our goals and values.
  • Full ownership of what we create outside of work: Wizards can currently claim ownership over any IP created by employees during their tenure at Wizards, including works that are fully unrelated to Wizards IP. What we make in our free time should belong to us, not the company."

Wargamer reached out to press representatives of Wizards of the Coast, and received a copy of an email apparently circulated to WotC staff in the US this week. In it, the firm announces its decision not to voluntarily recognize the union.

It couches the decision in terms of individual choice, stating "it is the right of every eligible employee to decide whether union representation is right for them". It adds that proceeding with a vote is the best way to give everyone affected an equal voice in the decision.

The email states that management believes "we are best able to keep building great games and a great place to work by working directly with employees, not through unions. In this regard, Wizards is not neutral on the question of unionization." However, "in the end, we will respect the results of the election, no matter what our employees choose". "We expect conversations to remain respectful and that no one will be treated differently based on where they stand", the email adds.

The email also lists achievements and benefits at the company which it says have been "accomplished together in direct collaboration".

  • "Individual Contributor average base salary in Wizards that is up 20% since 2023, well above external benchmarks
  • Annual bonuses including 200% of target in 2025
  • Five weeks of paid time off in addition to paid company break weeks and holidays
  • Heavily subsidized comprehensive medical benefits
  • Free product"

Along with Digital Gaming, Wizards of the Coast is the most profitable part of Hasbro. In its Q2 earnings report for 2026, Hasbro reports that  this year WotC and Digital Gaming have generated $568 million of pre-tax profit, while its 'Entertainment' division made $23 million, and 'Consumer Products' (toys) lost $62 million. In an official filing in April 2026, Hasbro disclosed that CEO Chris Cocks' full remuneration for 2025 was worth $18,672,521, a sum it estimated at 165 times the median pay for its staff.

Union staff in the US earn, on average, around 12.8% more than staff on individually negotiated contracts, according to the Economic Policy Institute.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Murdertalon Raiders
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific Detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Murdertalon Raiders Detachment for Chaos Space Marines.

Introduced in the deluge of 1 DP Detachments at the outset of 11th edition, the Murdertalon Raiders Detachment acts as a 1 DP boost for your Jump Pack units, aka Raptors and Warp Talons. Initially released with the Purge the Foe Disposition, the Murdertalon Detachment has since been adjusted to be Recon, in order to prevent it from being a cheap way to get access to Purge.

Disposition: Reconnaissance

Detachment Cost: 1 DP

Unique: NIGHTMARE

This Detachment focuses squarely on buffing your flying infantry units, with rules very similar to the bonuses you get from Nightmare Hunt, only for just these specific units. For that reason perhaps, this is one of the few Detachments with a relevant unique tag: The NIGHTMARE tag for this Detachment prevents it from being used alongside Nightmare Hunt - but notably not Dread Talons, and we'll talk about the potential there in the "Playing this Detachment" section. Otherwise the bonuses here are fine but ultimately tied to units you're just not really using - CSM jump infantry are nothing to write home about; Warp Talons are good when they're costed efficiently and right now they're not. Likewise Raptors are more durable and stronger than before but still too expensive for a unit that lacks re-rolls in melee built into its profile.

Detachment Rule: Prey on the Weak

There are two parts to this:

  • Friendly INFANTRY FLY units’ attacks targeting a unit that’s either battle-shocked or below half-strength can re-roll hit rolls of 1.
  • When enemy units target a friendly INFANTRY FLY unit, if the attacking unit is battle-shocked or below half-strength, they get -1 to their hit rolls.

That -1 to hit rolls debuff is pretty good in 11th edition, since it combines with cover to put units on -2, which can be devastating when you’re relying on a smaller number of high-damage attacks. That said, battle-shock is and always has been an unreliable mechanic and it’ll be scant consolation if you can’t manage to finish off a unit and it lingers at the below half strength mark. This is just OK but don’t be shocked if you forget you have it. The big challenge is that CSM lack good ways to force additional tests on enemy units outside of Raptors getting into melee, and you really don't want to throw your units into melee with a unit they're not likely to kill.

A lot of the value in this Detachment comes from the Enhancements and the Stratagems, which do have some very good bonuses for your Warp Talons and Raptors to play with. That said, those are just not great units to begin with, and so building around them feels pretty bad. When 11th edition first released, this Detachment looked fairly attractive as an add-on to Veterans of the Long War; that was because at the time taking a unit of 10 Warp Talons was very common in CSM lists as a unit you could Ingress onto the table, then use to charge and kill an enemy unit before leaving at the end of your opponent's turn. However Warp Talons have since then gone up in price and become less useful offensively (staying S5 as marines have gone up to T5), and with the new update, the Cabal of Chaos Detachment has become much, much better. The net result is that most CSM players tended to focus on 3 DP Detachments or other options, and Warp Talons do just fine with the buffs you get from Pactbound Zealots, Creations of Bile, or Veterans of the Long War.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

There are two options here, and they're both limited to Chaos Lords with Jump Packs.

  • Shadowcowl Talisman (20 points) - CHAOS LORD WITH JUMP PACK only. The unit has a 5+ Inv save. This is a neat upgrade for Raptors, who otherwise lack any kind of invulnerable save. That said, there’s a lot of AP-2 out there and not so much AP-3 so you may find the situations where you actually get to use this fairly rare. That said, it’s good enough when it does matter to be worth taking. If you're taking it, you want it with a unit of ten Raptors. Which you don't really want to take, and so you don't really want ot take this upgrade, tragically.
  • Pact of Cursed Pinions (20 points) - CHAOS LORD WITH JUMP PACK only. The model has the DAEMON keyword and gets +1 A on its melee attacks. This is fine. Chaos Lords can use the extra attack on their power fists. This model also gains the ability to join Warp Talons, which is listed in the MFM. That’s important, because it’s a great add-on to a unit of Warp Talons and without it, this enhancement is just worthless. 20 points is a lot for this, but getting the extra melee buff helps.

Stratagems

The Stratagems here are solid. They’re all priced at 1 CP, meaning you won’t have many issues around CP generation and you'll get real value out of bringing a Chaos Lord or two with you.

  • Plunging Talons (1 CP). Used in the Fight phase on an INFANTRY FLY unit that made a charge move this turn. They gain [LANCE] on their melee attacks. This is more or less the best thing about this Detachment. You’ve got a unit of 10 Warp Talons and now you can give them lance, letting them wound on a 2+ or 4+ against key targets and re-rolling all their wound rolls.
  • Raking Pass (1 CP). Used in your Movement phase, when a friendly INFANTRY FLY unit makes a Fall Back move. That unit can fall back and charge. This is also great - useful ability, great to have, re-triggers Plunging Talons. What’s not to love? In those rare times you get stuck in combat with a unit of Warp Talons, you can use this to fall back and find a newer, better target to assail.
  • Warp-Twisted Terrors (1 CP). Used in your Movement phase on a unit of Warp Talons finishing a move. Pick an enemy unit (excluding MONSTER/VEHICLE) within 9” of your unit. That unit has to take a battle-shock roll with -1 to that roll.  Out-of-phase testing is solid, but still unreliable. Being able to do this in the Movement phase is good however, and you can stack this with the -1 for a unit being within range of a unit of Warp Talons to put real pressure on enemy units.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

This is a tough Detachment to love. As a 1 DP add-on, it's competing with Cabal of Chaos, and now that the updates have hit and Terminators look way better, there just isn't much reason to take this one. That's also partly because the buff you actually get here on your Warp Talons and Raptors isn't very good, and if you're taking Warp Talons and playing them correctly, you're already spending 1 CP per round on them for Rapid Ingress, so even though the Plunging Talons Stratagem is good, it's not something you can spend on every single round.

So what are your options here? Well, if you're playing this it's for one of two reasons: Either you're trying to get more out of your Warp Talons as an add-on unit and don't want to run Cabal of Chaos, or it's because you're a Night Lords sicko trying to make them work as a full army.

Let's start with the first of those two scenarios. If you're running this to improve your Warp Talons, then chances are good you're running this Detachment alongside Veterans of the Long War because if you were taking Warpstrike Champions you'd be taking Cabal of Chaos instead for the Terminator buffs. Here you're going to be looking at a unit of Warp Talons led by a Chaos Lord with Pact of Cursed Pinions so you have the ability to drop the cost of your Rapid Ingress Stratagem with the Warp Talons, freeing them up to use Plunging Talons on a regular basis to kill harder targets. The math improves substantially when you add [LANCE] to the equation, and with full re-rolls to hit at 4+ it'll often make more sense to throw out [SUSTAINED HITS 1] instead of [LETHAL HITS] against those harder targets (4+ is the break-even point for lethal/sustained but sustained has higher potential upside; at 5+, stick to Lethals).

On the other hand if you're running Night Lords, well, you can't pair this with Nightmare Hunt so your option is basically Dread Talons. Dread Talons isn't a great Detachment, but it has some interesting things in it. Combining these two basically gives you a slight better(?) version of Nightmare Hunt, where you are forcing tests at units below Starting Strength, and at -1 to tests within 12". If you want to go as hard as possible, the play here becomes using Raptors, Dread Talons, and Noise Marines to stack -1 modifiers to Ld, then using the Warp-Twisted Terrors Stratagem to force tests at a whopping -4 in your Movement phase. These tend to be modifiers to the battle-shock roll, and so let you bypass that 9+ cap on Leadership modifiers - you're modifying the roll of the test, not the enemy Ld characteristic. Putting space marines on a 10+ is pretty great... but they're just going to un-battleshock on their turn. Go hard on Raptors - you want a unit of ten with a lord sporting Warp-Fuelled Thrusters and a second unit of ten sporting the Shadowcowl Talisman - then fill out the rest of your army with good units that get almost nothing out of being in an army with these Detachments.

Strengths

  • Warp Talons. You get some awesome buffs to your warp talons here - being able to attach Chaos Lords and have [LANCE] are both great benefits.

Weaknesses

  • Narrow benefits. This really only does anything for your Warp Talons, with a few benefits for Raptors. Those aren't units to build an entire army around, and Raptors have been living right on the edge of playability for a while now.

Final Thoughts

If you're taking this Detachment, the best place is with Veterans of the Long War, where you're running a generically strong Detachment with good rules and making one of your key pieces - Warp Talons - even better. It's a fun little Detachment, but losing Purge the Foe really hurts and it just can't combine with any of the other Detachments where you'd really want to take Warp Talons or Raptors, making it a tough sell.

title: 11th Edition Detachment Focus: Purestrain Broodswarm
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Purestrain Broodswarm Detachment for Genestealer Cults. 

Purestrain Broodswarm continues the trend of strong Detachments that are efficient in the buffs they offer while hitting key units within the army that are happy to receive them. I'll give Games Workshop its flowers when they've earned them: This is one of the most transformative Detachments in the game right now thanks to the upgrades it offers, and I think any pilot will be happy to have this toolbox at the ready.

Purestrain Broodswarm

Detachment Points: 1 DP

Force Disposition: Priority Assets

Unique: PURESTRAIN

Priority Assets is a staple in the current meta of Warhammer 40k and most Detachments will be happy to see it as their force disposition. Generally, just needing a unit to walk out and perform an action while holding your natural expansion will walk you up to that 45 primary limit by the end of the game, and such a low-resource task is great for most armies; that being said, the utility offered in this detachment makes that even easier.

Detachment Rule: Enemy Within

At the end of your opponent’s fight phase any unengaged Purestrain Genestealers (PSG) can be placed in Strategic Reserves. This Detachment has the PURESTRAIN tag and cannot be taken with other Detachments with the same tag.

This rule really helps PSG get around the board and move from flank to flank. It’s a bit more difficult to just pick them up and charge back in, but honestly, just moving a five-man unit around to do actions or score your mission cards is excellent as-is. Having the Patriarch squad be able to go up at the end of T1 to threaten a nasty T2 rapid ingress if your opponent plays cagey is great. Combined with Priority Assets, five PSG can easily be your best action units in the game while the 10s gain versatility in their threat projection.

As a sidenote, GSC continues to kill it with the cool names for most of their rules and I just like how fitting this is for PSG.

Purestrain Genestealers: Who's ready for razor hugs?
Credit: Pendulin

Enhancements

So nice of GW to include a second enhancement next to the only one you need so it doesn’t get lonely.

  • Mark of the Star Children (Upgrade 30pts): PSG unit only. Models in the unit gain +1 Strength, +1 Toughness, and a 4+ armor save.  It’s so insanely expensive but it’s so insanely good too. Being able to upgrade up to 30 PSG to be S5/T5 is game changing and makes them much bigger threats into a lot of the meta right now. However, with all of that being said I still think this needs to come down by 15 points if I can be so bold.
  • Talons of the Sire (15 pts): Patriarch model only. This unit’s attacks can re-roll 1s to wound. It’s not mark and you’re taking mark on every PSG unit so this enhancement doesn’t matter. At time of writing you can’t stack 2 enhancements/upgrades onto a unit, so until then this enhancement doesn’t exist. If you could, yes, you would 100% take this on a Patriarch leading a Marked PSG squad.
I now realise I should have made one with two heads

Stratagems

  • Inhuman Reactions (1 CP): During your opponent’s movement phase, when an enemy unit ends a move within 8” of a PSG unit, that unit can make a reactive move of D3+3”. A very solid stratagem and makes it so that even if a player ends their movement just outside of 2” of the PSG unit, they could potentially be looking at a 7” charge minimum if the unit goes straight back. Overall, an amazing tool to have access to.
  • Crawling Horror (1CP): Give a PSG unit -6” detection range for the turn. The timing on this is rough; instead of being in the shooting phase, it is within the movement phase, so you can’t reactive move and then pop a 9” detection range, unfortunately. Still has its place, but pretty easy to play around since it’s also declared at the start of the phase.
  • Lurk and Strike (1CP): Fallback and charge for a PSG unit. Being able to deny your opponent from tagging you up with some kind of Rhino or durable piece is a great tool to have and I have even used this after a heroic from a PSG squad in my opponent’s previous turn to help rocket PSG up the board. The skill expression here goes a bit deeper than you might think on the tin and I think that’s just great.
Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

Truly this is the melee player's divine heaven: Three amazing stratagems to help control your opponent’s ability to interact with your melee pieces, a noticeable output and defensive increase for said unit, and the ability to use them as a utility piece as well really cements this Detachment as one of the strongest 1 pointers in the game. It still only affects basically one datasheet so it’s not game changing like Librarius or Lords of the Forge, but I think this is what the power level other 1 pointers should strive to be at.

Strengths

  • Mobility. Access to return to reserves on the Detachment rules, native advance and charge, AND access to both a reactive move or fallback and charge is just everything you could want in a melee-focused Detachment.
  • Strength. Listen, 40 attacks at S5 AP-2 Damage1 isn’t world ending but it is respectable, and the ability to couple that with increased longevity thanks to the T5 breakpoint makes these units amazing amongst other skirmishing threats.

Weaknesses

  • Cost. 30 points is so much. Especially since you want to really bring multiple units of these and even the 5s like the upgrade so you’re often times dropping 60-90 points in the Detachment. It’s a genuine investment that’s only saved by being able to recur the unit through Cult Ambush.
  • Power Ceiling. Unfortunately this just doesn’t compete with the most broken things going on in the game right now for its points cost. Do you want to pay 250 points for a Patriarch and 10 upgraded PSG, or do you want to save 40 points and just buy 10 Flash Gitz? Maybe I’m being crazy but if I dropped 40 points to pick up some melta shots I think that would be pretty good.

A Sample List

Since the start of 11th I’ve had it in the back of my head that the Codices were going to be trying this new triple 1 point Detachment style of list building and I wanted to get in on it early. So, as soon as the new edition dropped I started slamming down a list archetype I lovingly refer to as PXH as a combination of all three 1 point Detachments GSC got in the new edition. The list has been the most fun I’ve had playing in the new edition and I would greatly recommend trying out this wacky build that somehow all works together despite not having any overlap. Enjoy!

ATTACHED UNITS

  • Attached as: Leader (Character)

title: [40K] Tabletop Battles Hot Take: The October 14 Warhammer App Updates
content:
Games Workshop released a series of updates today to both the FAQs on Warhammer-Community and through their Warhammer 40k app, changing datasheets and rules here and there, making some key changes and a few obvious mistakes. There’s a lot of little stuff, and as usual, we’ve got the full rundown here with what it means.

Core Rules: The extra CP you get for having a specific Warlord in an 11th edition Codex stops working when the Warlord is destroyed.

This is how most people were playing the game already, and is extremely sensible.

Core Rules: Firing Deck does not get any enhancements, rules, or abilities from the donor unit, no matter the wording on the source.

Flash Git enthusiasts are in shambles. Previously, some people thought that there was a significant distinction between “Weapons equipped by models in this unit” and “This unit’s weapons have,” and this FAQ confirms that you only transfer the base weapon to the transport when you use the Firing Deck rule.

Core Rules: Units that Rapid Disembark cannot be targeted with Heroic Intervention.

More of a confirmation rather than a change, as Rapid Disembark already prevents you from declaring a charge the turn you do it, but this helps stop any Ork shenanigans they can do with the reactive disembark from their Trukks.

Core Rules: When you replace a model with another, you need to center it where the original model was.

Another sensible clarification; this will stop someone from getting cheeky and attempting to gain a significant movement advantage replacing a model on the edge of where the original model was.

Core Rules: A line has no thickness and is straight.

Your 10th grade teacher always told you basic geometry would be used in your future and you didn’t listen.

Core Rules: Rules that say you take or re-roll Desperate Escape tests have been cleaned up.

Before it was a little unclear exactly how these 10th edition rules worked in 11th, and now it is clarified that having to take a Desperate Escape test means you have to pick that fall-back mode, and re-rolling means you re-roll the hazard tests. 

Adepta Sororitas: The Desperate for Redemption Detachment Rule now triggers at the start of your Command phase, not the Battle Round.

The only real change here is that your Absolution in Battle (+1 Attack/Strength on the charge) and Death Before Disgrace (2+ fight on death) won’t be active on the first turn of the game if you’re going second. It also means you’re less likely to forget.

Adepta Sororitas: The Triumph of St. Katherine Solemn Procession ability happens at the start of your turn.

A datasheet change in the app has changed this ability to happen at the start of your turn, not the start of the Battle Round. So you’ll only get that extra Miracle Dice on your turn - you won’t have it on your opponent’s turn if you’re going second.

Adeptus Mechanicus: The Luminen Auto-choir Detachment's The Chant of Electrotraction Stratagem was corrected.

This now affects a friendly ELECTRO-PRIESTS unit instead of an ELECTRO-PRIESTS BATTLECLADE unit, fixing an obvious error.

Adeptus Mechanicus: Haloscreed Battle Clade Detachment's Guided Retreat Stratagem changed.

The language here was cleaned up to reflect the changes to re-rolling Hazardous rolls.

Adeptus Custodes: Superior Creation now Once Per Battle, Per Army.

You only live twice.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Aeldari: Agile Manoeuvres Sudden Strike only triggers when a unit from your army ends a charge move.

You can only use the Sudden Strike ability for a 6” pile-in or consolidation move after making a charge move with that unit. This is a small nerf, preventing you from getting good defensive pile-ins with large or spread-out units.

Aeldari: Seer Council Unshrouded Truth Stratagem now specifies that you must make the ingress move in your first turn.

This clarifies that your unit must be set back up in the same turn, even if it’s on the first turn of the game (when ingress moves are normally prohibited).

Aeldari: Ride the Wind Detachment Rule allows for first-turn ingress moves.

An FAQ item clarifies that the Detachment rule here also applies to Ingress moves made with your MOUNTED/VYPER units, allowing you to make them during the first battle round.

Blood Angels: The Death Company Captain is handed the plush Tomy Power Fist.

In what is assuredly a mistake, the Death Company Captain’s Powerfist was given the statline of a standard Sergeant’s Power Fist, i.e. three attacks, hitting on a 3+. Hopefully this gets reverted quickly. But until then, it’s pretty funny.

Imperial Agents: The Callidus Assassin loses [PRECISION] and gained [BLAST 2] on her Neural Shredder Weapon.

This is more of a housekeeping change in the sense that [TORRENT] weapons can’t have [PRECISION] in 11th edition, which made the rule worthless for the Callidus. Swapping that out for [BLAST 2] continues a trend we’ve been seeing in new codexes to give flamers and other torrent weapons BLAST and a smaller number of shots (though notably she kept D6). This represents a buff overall on the Callidus, and having D6+4 shots of ANTI-INFANTRY 2+ shooting into a 10-model unit is pretty nasty.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Leagues of Votann: Arkanyst Evaluators don’t give each other Lone Operative.

An added FAQ item specifies that you need a non-Arkanyst model within 3” to get Lone Operative via the Science Guild Support ability.

Orks: Wazbom Blastajet base size updated.

This one’s in the tournament companion - your blastajet should be on a 120x92mm oval base.

Space Marines: Fixed some lingering errors.

A few lingering errors for Codex Space Marines were fixed, such as Cato Sicarius having the wrong Attack and Strength counts on some of his attacks - these now reflect the updated stats in the new Codex. Likewise for the Captain in Phobos Armour, whose gun had the incorrect stats. All of the Jump Pack equipped characters now can join the correct Vanguard Veterans, instead of the foot-bound Legends version. On the Dark Angels side, Belial can be attached to Terminator Assault Squads, an obvious oversight. For Black Templars, Chaplain Grimaldus is actually a Chaplain, and the Marshal and Castellan’s weapons are fixed.

Space Marines: Kayvaan Shrike has the EPIC HERO keyword.

This fixes an obvious error - our boy Kevin is one of a kind. Note that this change is not reflected in the 40k app yet, but it can be found in the Printed Products Updates document found on Warhammer Community.

Space Marines (Deathwatch): Decimus Kill Team gains Tacticus and Gravis keywords.

The Decimus Kill Team is a strange mix of armour types, and before didn’t have any armour keywords. Now each model type has their respective keyword, except for the Phobos guy, who gets Tacticus for some reason. This will impact how well they fit into a Rhino, and opens up new synergies with how the unit can interact with the Tacticus and Gravis detachments.

Tyranids: Biovores don’t lose hidden when launching Seed Spore Mines.

Another FAQ item. This isn’t a shooting attack, so your Biovore stays hidden, like a coward.

Final Thoughts

After years of clamoring for digital rules, we’ve actually started to come around to the nastier side of that: A world where the app is the only source of truth for the game, but the data going into it is often wrong or it’s poorly-coded, meaning that even when something is obviously wrong, it’s still the truth for the game. If you’re building a list right now, Kayvaan Shrike can still be added multiple times without breaking validation, and Death Company Captains shouldn’t be swinging 3 power fist attacks, but here we are.

Otherwise, these changes are fine. 

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. And don’t forget that you can support us on Patreon for backer rewards like early video content, Administratum access, an ad-free experience on our website and more.
