title: Star Wars X-Wing designer talks about his new mecha wargame - "People want to feel like they're in the cockpit"
content:
Star Wars X-Wing may be out of production, but its legacy lives on, with fan communities continuing to support the game, and exciting new projects from former designers. I spoke to Max Brooke, a former Fantasy Flight Games designer who worked on both editions of X-Wing, to learn about his upcoming new game Precipice - a mech piloting wargame designed to make you feel like you're really in the cockpit.

Brooke joined FFG as an RPG producer in 2011, doing everything from project management to game design for the Warhammer 40k RPG and Star Wars RPG. "Because we were all mini gamers, the RPG team members often served as playtesting pitch-hitters for the growing miniatures department". That began with Dust, FFG's first miniature wargame, before the team "participated in some of the Wave 1 playtests" for X-Wing and "the early testing of Star Wars: Armada".

An opening appeared for Brooke in the Miniatures design team "around five years into my time at FFG", and he "stepped into a design role on X-Wing for Wave 9 of 1st edition", including the Shadow Caster, Fang Fighter, TIE/sf, and ARC-170. "The first wave was sort of an apprenticeship under Alex Davy and Frank Brooks".

If you played first edition, you might recognize some of Brooke's work. "One of the first upgrades I designed was Seismic Torpedoes" - single-use weapons that turn asteroids into clouds of deadly debris. "Destructible terrain has always been something I've enjoyed", Brooke says - it shows up substantially in Precipice. In subsequent waves he worked "on ships like the Quadjumper and Skurrg Heavy Bomber, which had interesting movement and position considerations of their own".

As he recalls it, "One of the challenges of X-Wing 1st Edition was that the design space was incredibly tight. There were barely any levers to pull, and you had to really think outside the box to create interesting new content".

Brooke worked on the X-Wing 2nd Edition refresh, which he calls "an amazing opportunity to revisit everything we'd all learned about the game and bring together an edition with the design space to last as long as we needed it to". That included carving out faction identities with specific design ideas, and "assessing which fundamentals we wanted to elevate (flying the ships, rewarding positioning) and what game design elements of 1st Edition had impeded those things".

Brooke's involvement with Armada was much lighter. "I never had much formal involvement beyond helping playtest and sitting in on brainstorming sessions as a member of the Miniatures team", he says. "But I did get to work closely with Michael Gernes and Brooks Flugaur-Leavitt, both of whom are friends to this day and close collaborators on Precipice!"

Precipice

Brooke is in the early stages of playtesting Precipice, an original wargame inspired by mecha anime. Some of its X-Wing DNA is immediately apparent. A lot like X-Wing, players build and load out their mechs with rules cards, starting with a core body, then attaching cards for limbs and a head, and equipping those sections with weapons. The game uses a similar action programming sequence, with each player locking in a sequence of commands that their pilot is feeding to their mech before revealing their plans to one another.

But there's an even more fundamental, and unusual, feature of the game that owes its origins to X-Wing - "the spotlight is always on one unit". Precipice is a game of duelling mech pilots, with players typically controlling just one model (or two, for those scenarios when mechs can exit their vehicles, Titanfall style). Brooke says the "the biggest influence in this regard" were his "experiences watching people play X-Wing".

"Consistently, from the most casual tables to the top table at Worlds, players just love flying the ships", Brooke says. "Ace lists, in which players would focus on a pair of ships, or even a single ship with a disposable wingmate, made up an incredibly popular playstyle". "Strategic and tactical level games are fun, but I could tell X-Wing was scratching a different itch for a lot of people", Brooke says, "People want to feel like they're in the cockpit".

Despite the popularity of ace lists, X-Wing's design still assumed that players would control multiple units. But seeing the appeal of this playstyle - and recognizing it as something he wanted to get involved with - set Brooke wondering: "could a game be fun with just one primary piece on the table?"

Brooke thinks that it can, "but it pays to start thinking expansively about what a game piece is in a miniatures game". Precipice doesn't just have rules for destructible terrain, they're a key factor of the design. "This is partly because it's fun to have your mech smash buildings", Brooke says, "but it's also because it's good for the gameplay loop to have numerous things to interact with on the table - the game gets more interesting if your actions might have larger consequences than you originally intend".

"Thinking of the battlefield as a set of resources and threats (rather than as a set of modifiers) was critical to designing a game with a single primary miniature", he adds.

I've not yet playtested Precipice, but the rules suggest that you're going to really feel the weight of the machine under your command. As mechs start lumbering in a direction they build up momentum which will keep them moving the same way at the end of the turn. Even if your piloting is good, your opponent's unpredictable actions could result in that momentum sending you into the side of a building or through a fuel silo as they knock you off your original course. Taking a particularly hectic turn will see you commit multiple action cards to your mech, but if you pull back more than three cards you'll apply damaging strain to your mech's chassis.

"I want both the fun and the challenge of Precipice to be the control of the mech", Brooke says. "Most mecha miniatures games put the player into a "command and control" role, and abstract a lot of the piloting", he continues. "For an army-based game, that's a totally reasonable design decision. But I wanted to do something different with Precipice - I don't just want to make a game about mechs, I want to make a game about piloting mechs."

This is the other half of Precipice's heritage - Brooke is a huge fan of mecha. "One of my biggest inspirations was my early experience playing MechWarrior 3", he says, "It was hard to get the mech to do what I wanted, but it was incredibly rewarding when it worked!" In other sim games, "from later MechWarrior entries to Strike Suit Zero to Gundam: Battle Operation 2, I noticed that there was often intentional friction inserted into the way the game played, forcing you to consider your moves in advance of trying to execute them".

That friction between your intentions and the tools you have to execute on them "resonated with what a lot of people reported liking about both X-Wing and Armada". Brookes says he hopes Precipice will have "somewhat less friction than I had with MechWarrior, but I want people to feel like they're improving, mastering the system, and becoming more adept as pilots as they play".

Along with the rules, Brooke is working with collaborators to develop miniatures for the game, "first as STLs for home 3d printing, and hopefully in other forms in the future", he says. "Getting to see the original designs for the game realized is utterly magical, and the artists and sculptors I've had the pleasure of working with are an amazing bunch!", he adds, but "as excited as I am about our original designs, the game is very much meant to be playable as a "Bring Your Own Mech" experience, too". "Part of the reason I wanted to make this game was that I have a lot of amazing kits I'd love to put on the table, if only I had a game where they really fit in."

If you're intrigued by Precipice, you can get all the playtest documents for the open alpha at the Precipice website.  Signing up for the mailing list also gets you access to the Playtest Discord to meet likeminded players. If you give it a shot, hop on over to the Wargamer Discord community and let us know what you think!

title: The rarest and most expensive Lorcana cards of 2026
content:
What are the rarest, most expensive Lorcana cards? When the characters and films are so beloved by so many, it only makes sense mega-fans are prepared to shell out for a rare Disney card with unique art of their favorite character. This guide covers all the most expensive Disney Lorcana card sales from the most recent sets.

Disney Lorcana may be the newest of the big trading card games, but it has a dedicated fanbase of collectors who will pay a princess' ransom to get their hands on the most coveted cards. Older TCGs may have higher price ceilings - nothing on this list can match the most expensive rare Pokémon cards or expensive Yugioh Cards - but there are some very valuable cards nonetheless! The most expensive Lorcana cards are:

Elsa, Spirit of Winter (Enchanted) - $860

The original Elsa from 2023's The First Chapter set is already a collectible card, but this full art Enchanted variant is in another league. She's a double threat - not just one of the most popular Disney characters of all time, but the first card printed of that character when the game launched. If you've got one, don't let it go…

Merida - Formidable Archer (Iconic) - $930

We all know that Lorcana is a pacifist game, and nobody involved in a challenge is ever hurt - but we have to wonder what Merida does with her arrows to keep her opponents from getting hurt! This is one of the most dynamic princes poses in all of Lorcana - and still valuable, though the value has halved since this card came out.

Belle and Beast, Certain as the Sun (Iconic) - $930

A card as romantic as this was destined to be sought after - Belle and Beast waltzing is a timeless scene from the film that kicked off the Disney Renaissance.  They're also remarkably faithful to their original on-screen appearance as well. This is another that sank big-time in September. It used to be worth over $2,000!

Pocahontas - Peacekeeper (Iconic) - $1,150

The incredible multi-colored foiling on this card really does paint with all the colors of the wind. Pocahontas has never looked so noble - or so snug in that gorgeous coat!

Hades, Looking for a Deal (Iconic) - $1,200

This is currently the rarest Disney villain card around! Though released alongside the previous Pocahontas in winterwear, and just as rare, this card took a lot longer to rise to the heights. Maybe it's because Hades isn't a princess? Still, this sneaky backstabber spent all of August closing the distance, and finally overtook her just before the month ended.

Moana, Curious Explorer (Iconic) - $1,120

Moana was a surprise appearance in Winterspell, a set with a Winter theme, and it seems this explorer's curiosity is so great she didn't have time to dress for the colder weather. Nevertheless, this paper-cut inspired artwork is absolutely adorable, and helps to make this Iconic card so legendary.

Lilo and Stitch, Fun-Loving Friends (Iconic) - $1,400

There's so much energy and mischief in this Lilo and Stitch card. It looks like the box art for a straight-to-DVD sequel to the classic movie, and we mean that with love: there's no way any actual animation could live up to the sheer action this promises!

Winnie the Pooh, Hunny Wizard (Enchanted) - $1,450

The colors here are making us so hungry. Pooh Bear doesn't have any fancy abilities to show off, but he does have a soothing smile, a fancy cloak, and golden, sugary goodness surrounding him. Those base stats aren't too shabby, either. By the end of August, Winnie the Pooh was getting close to Ariel, after a long time jockeying for position with Moana.

Ariel, Ethereal Voice (Iconic) - $1,550

This ghostly 'Whisper' of Ariel from the Whispers in the Well set not only has a commanding performance, she also commands a high price on the secondary market, which has only crept up since she released.

Buzz Lightyear, Jungle Ranger (Iconic) - $1,850

When Wilds Unknown released Buzz Lightyear quickly became the second most valuable card you can open in a booster pack. Now it's distinctly finite, though still among the top three Lorcana cards of all time.

Mickey Mouse, Brave Little Prince (Iconic) - $2,500

Surprisingly, Mickey is now not doing better than Minnie. There are precious few copies in circulation, and the market price seems to fluctuate between $2,500 and $3,000.

Minnie Mouse, Sweetheart Princess (Iconic) - $4,200

When the first Iconic cards were created for Lorcana they were immediately way pricier than anything else on the market, and nearly made it into the all-time top 10, up against extremely rare early promos. Minnie, blowing a kiss in her medieval princess garb, was beginning to slip from her initial high position on the list - but made a recovery in late August as a sheer lack of supply drove up the market price. By October, she was back with a vengeance, even outstripping Mickey!

If you're a Lorcana collector but not yet a player, you should fix that immediately! It's easy to learn, and we can talk you through which Lorcana starter decks are worth playing.

title: Why is Lugia EX suddenly the #5 most costly Pokémon card of all time?
content:
A copy of Lugia EX from the Black and White era Pokémon TCG set Plasma Storm has just sold for a staggering $660,000. The sale took place on October 12, 2026 on the auction site Fanatics Collect and it appears to be the largest sum of money anyone has ever spent on this particular card.

Which is not that surprising. $660k is an astonishing sum, instantly rocketing this card up to number 5 on our expensive rare Pokémon cards guide, behind all-time greats like Illustrator Pikachu and Base set Charizard.

What would make someone want to spend so much on this card? Well, it's a PSA 10, one of only 21 in existence, according to the online auction house. And it depicts an awesome Legendary Pokémon, king of the original legendary birds. But that doesn't explain why investors are chomping at the bit for this particular version.

While cards like Crystal Lugia from the far older set Aquapolis have traditionally been a lot more famous and more valuable, Lugia EX has exploded in price over the last two years, particularly ramping up this year. In January 2025, a PSA 9 copy would sell for 'only' $350. Now, you'd be fortunate to find one for $4,000.

Fans have been watching this particular Fanatics Collect auction with interest, as the bids grew to more and more ridiculous heights. At one point it was even over $10 million, but it seems like there were many bogus bids. In the end, it sold for a fraction of that price, but still a crazy figure.

While the card is in relatively short supply at this grade, there are certainly rarer cards that are far less expensive. The foiling, pose, and Plasma logo all combine to make a pretty sweet card - it would look great in a binder - but at the end of the day there's no straightforward explanation for this monumental increase.

Of course, this sudden spike, and the changing values on this auction, has led to lots of accusations of market manipulation - someone deliberately trying to raise a card's profile so they can offload lots of copies. But there's no evidence that this is what has occurred.

title: As D&D staff fight to unionize, Project Lamordia reads like a cry for help
content:
To steal a phrase from Critical Role, I can't prove this is allegory. It's unlikely that the Dungeons and Dragons design team released a new module just to make a political statement. But, boy, is it hard not to read into Project_Lamordia. D&DBeyond's new scifi Ravenloft module has some eerie parallels to the real-life labor issues at Wizards of the Coast.

Last week, D&D and MTG staff announced plans to unionize. A public petition announced their wish to join United Wizards of the Coast, a union formed by MTG Arena employees in partnership with Communication Workers of America. MTGA staff successfully voted to unionize in June, and now this new team wants Wizards to publicly recognize their union - something, as October 14, the union says Wizards has refused to do.

The union petition states many goals for United Wizards of the Coast. Participating staff seek fair wages, job security, remote work, protection from crunch, and accessible healthcare. They also call for "protection against the encroachment of AI" (which, given how often Hasbro CEO Chris Cocks espouses its usefulness, seems entirely fair), as well as "full ownership of what we create outside of work".

Bear this in mind while I summarize Project_Lamordia.

"The pain will be temporary," the doctor says, "but your contributions to science shall be everlasting."

This is a digital D&D module that reinvents Lamordia, a popular Ravenloft domain, as a modern scifi horror. Mordenheim Kinetics, a research facility from a place called Gothic Earth, is a cutting-edge tech company. It was once a playground for egotistical scientists, corporate leaders, and their rich investors. However, the Mists of Ravenloft have turned it into a maze of ruined, haunted labs and offices.

The Darklord at the heart of all this is CEO Viktra Mordenheim. She's a top expert on AI, cybernetic augmentation, and memory transplants. She also, according to the module, "forced her employees to work long hours and under increasingly unsafe conditions". Her quest to find immortality led to the deaths of many, including a former lover, who reported her unethical labor practices - and was murdered for his efforts. Adam, an animatronic with some of his memories, now roams the halls.

Viktra is still served by a few unlucky employees who became trapped when the Mists rose (in fact, Viktra locked the gates and refused to let any of them leave). Among her retinue are the von Aubrecker siblings, three high-level scientists who have augmented themselves beyond humanity. Each of them is a bastion of corporate malpractice. Take, for example, this quote about Rudolph von Aubrecker: "In his singleminded pursuit of his research, he has committed countless atrocities-and he will surely commit more."

The entire adventure has an underlying theme, and it's a lack of autonomy. Viktra and the Aubreckers have filled their abandoned lab with Echoes and Created, automatons who contain the neuroprint and memories of a real person. The creation of these creatures is a brutal, painful process, and they're prone to confusion and dangerous malfunction. They're also unable to leave Mordenheim Kinetics.

I won't say much more, because I don't want to spoil this adventure for those that want to play. It's a well-written Gothic tale with a lot of interesting new ideas, from a new Survivor player mode to additional feats and monsters. The horror of Mordenheim Kinetics hits hard, because we can all relate to the fears it taps into. The world kind of sucks, and we're pretty sure AI is making it worse instead of better - that's as true anywhere else as it is at Wizards of the Coast.

Project_Lamordia credits Patrick Renie with its game design, with additional design provided by Joey Haeck and F. Wesley Schneider. Haeck is among the staff that have publicly supported union efforts, as is Project_Lamordia producer Vanessa Hoskins.

You can support the union efforts by signing United Wizards of the Coast's petition. If you'd like to talk more about D&D, you can also join the conversation in our official Wargamer Discord.

title: Classic MTG artists trick your brain in perhaps the best Secret Lair of 2026
content:
Your mind isn't playing tricks on you, this is just the latest Magic: The Gathering Secret Lair, and by Bolas' weird little beard, it's a fine one. Shown off with surprisingly little ceremony on October 13, Wizards has prepared a fine gimmick for this batch of premium cards. Four artists responsible for some of the most famous cards in Magic history redesigned their pieces for entirely different cards, and the result creates a strange feeling in the brain.

For instance, Mercadian Masques' Brainstorm piece by DiTerlizzi is reimagined as Thought Seize, featuring a similar mage with rather different headgear doing exactly the same pose. There are even Alpha cards here. Mark Poole's original Counterspell is now Pyroblast (that poor wizard finally got to cast his spell!), while Sandra Everingham's Dark Ritual is redrawn for Desperate Ritual.

Tribute to the World Tree sticks out as not really being a mirror of its counterpart from Legends, Phil Foglio's Presence of the Master. Famously that card has an uncanny resemblance to Albert Einstein, so I kind of wish they'd stuck Marie Curie or Ada Lovelace on the new version. I don't think this white-haired, white-eyed woman is a reference to any historical figure.

At any rate, this is a great Secret Lair in concept and execution, and the card choice isn't bad either. All of these cards are worth more than $5, so even though there's only four of them, the total value still comes out at around $35.

1/4

A little frustratingly, this is a Chaos Vault product, which means it's liable to launch suddenly and with little warning or marketing at a relatively random time. You'll need to have your eye on the ball to capture this Lair, named 'Duality Distorted', before it's all sold out.

In other SL news, Wizards of the Coast opened orders on its 'Corn Maze superdrop' yesterday, and some of the more popular collections are already all gone. Head to the Secret Lair website to scope them out for yourself, or give our October superdrop price breakdown a look - we'll let you know whether each one is a good deal or a rip off.

Also, yes, Nicol Bolas has a beard, or at the very least a very peculiar chin.

title: Warhammer 40k Boltgun 2 dev promises "bloodthirst and rage" from its new daemon enemies
content:
The original Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun was an unexpected classic, a high-octane retro FPS that pitted the player against relentless hordes of pixellated cultists, Chaos Space Marines, and the daemon servants of the ruinous powers. With the sequel Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 due to release the same day this article drops, I took the opportunity to interview lead designer Matt Bone to learn how the sequel has taken the forces of Chaos to new extremes.

Warhammer 40k Boltgun has a well-deserved place on Wargamer's guide to the best Warhammer 40k games ever, but it was very much a first stab at the concept, with loads of potential foes left on the table. Notably, protagonist Malum Caedo only fought the daemonic servants of two of the four Chaos Gods, the plaguefather Nurgle and lord of magic and deceit Tzeentch. It was a bit like the Doom Slayer revving up the chainsaw, only to find that the Hell Knights, Cacodemons, and Pinkies were on strike.

Boltgun 2 brings in the forces of the missing gods: Khorne, the lord of slaughter, and Slaanesh, prince of excess. "We were keen to give each faction its own identity and feel, which extends to how the enemies behave in the game", Bone says. Most Chaos Daemons are melee combatants, so creating distinctive enemy behaviours that stopped them feeling samey "was on our minds from the earliest parts of development".

"For Khorne, we've leant into their bloodthirst and rage: Bloodletters leap directly at the player, swords held aloft; Berzerkers are true to their name, enraging at low health and aggressively engaging the player at every opportunity". "Khorne enemies definitely aren't ones for subtlety", Bone adds.

That differentiates them from Slaanesh, whose daemons "are more elusive and cunning - they're like predators playing with their prey". As Bone puts it, "Daemonettes don't come directly for the player, they leap around the battlefield, showing off their graceful prowess". They'll engage by closing the "gap with a rapid, zig-zagging phase attack", finally revealing "their true, horrifying appearance".

Picking which enemies to include was "an almost impossible choice, as there's so many in the Warhammer 40,000 universe". The original Boltgun has some deep cuts from the Warhammer IP, including the Plague Toad (which GW no longer makes models or rules for), and a design for the Exalted Flamer of Tzeentch based on a model produced in the 1990s.

Picking which of the many different versions of the daemons meant looking "into different variants of that enemy in terms of loadouts and appearance, figuring out which is the best fit for the game". "Again, we're usually spoilt for choice here", Bone says. Turning them into sprites is a collaborative process, "communicating with the Warhammer team to gain additional insight into how these enemies should look and behave in the game".

The returning enemies from the original Boltgun have received "a new coat of paint to bring them up to the level of the new enemies", and "in a lot of cases, we've improved their behaviour, whilst staying faithful to what people liked about them in the previous game". Bone gives the example of the Aspiring Champion - a relentless pursuer that follows you around like satan's charity mugger - who now has "a new sprint to make him even more terrifying (sorry, everyone)".

The new enemies and rebalancing "means we've been able to provide a lot more variety in the gameplay, which is one of our main goals with Boltgun 2", Bone says. "An encounter with Daemonettes leaping about whilst Noise Marines fire large, rebounding sonic projectiles from a distance is going to feel and play differently to one with Nurgle enemies covering the floor with toxic slime, the bullet hell of Tzeentch encounters, or Khorne enemies getting in your face".

The original Boltgun's combat encounters and arenas were generally excellent, but it had some brick walls of difficulty - the early Plague Toad boss fight was a real player filter, incredibly hard to kill and supported by repeatedly spawning hordes of disruptive Nurglings and long-ranged cultists. "We've learned a ton from what players have told us they liked and disliked about Boltgun 1", Bone says.

The team "sought to address the criticisms, making sure there's a lot more variety, and leaning into interesting mechanics rather than having bullet sponge enemies". "Our job has been to find the most engaging combinations for encounters", he adds, "but sometimes it's also about paring things back: there's an early encounter with a horde of Poxwalkers (a new enemy in Boltgun 2) that works because it's just them - albeit a hell of a lot of them".

If you pick up Boltgun 2, share your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Games Workshop Accidentally Leaks New Dwarf Faction for Age of Sigmar
content:
Games Workshop has a new dwarf faction headed to Age of Sigmar — and we know that because the company accidentally showed it off early.

The Khazalite Holds briefly appeared on the Irish version of the Warhammer Store website before being hastily taken down. GW hasn’t released high-resolution versions of the images, so for now fans are squinting at blurry screenshots. The company also hasn’t commented further on the leak itself.

What We Know So Far

Age of Sigmar already has two duardin factions — the steampunk air pirates of the Kharadron Overlords and the slayer-inspired Fyreslayers — but neither scratches the itch for classic Warhammer dwarves. The Khazalite Holds look set to change that.

The leaked images showed off three distinct groups of miniatures:

  • Footsoldiers — Stoic, unrelenting infantry with shields bearing traditional runes that Warhammer Fantasy veterans will recognise
  • Golem-like constructs — A trio of heavy hitters, described by one observer as “stout as all hell,” armed with greathammers and looking every bit the linebreakers
  • A leader — Thick armour, well-plaited hair, a billowing cloak, a great axe, and an impressive headpiece. Plus a tactical rock, naturally.

The models feature pseudo-Nordic knotwork and runic designs straight out of the Old World, but with the proportions and round bases that Age of Sigmar players are used to.

GW Responds to the Leak

Rather than waiting for Friday’s Big Autumn Warhammer Preview, GW leaned into the leak and shared a bit more about the faction.

“Meet a Gholem of Gazul,” the company said. “What’s a Gholem? Who is Gazul? Well, for now all we can say is that it marches to war amidst the war throngs of the Khazalites Holds – an all-new Duardin faction for Warhammer Age of Sigmar. We’ll delve into the lore, rules and even more sweet new miniatures on Friday in the live reveal show.”

So lore, rules, and more miniatures are all coming at the end of the week.

The Rumours Were Right

This one didn’t come out of nowhere. Drolf Ironhead, a hero from Warhammer Quest: Darkwater released earlier this year, had already hinted that a faction like this might be on the way. The leaked web images confirmed what fans had been speculating about for months.

Why Fans Are Excited

For longtime Warhammer players, this feels like a homecoming. The Old World’s classic dwarves have been missing from Age of Sigmar, and the Khazalite Holds look like a proper spiritual successor — much like how the Lumineth Realm-lords gave High Elf fans a new home in the Mortal Realms.

The full reveal is expected at Friday’s live show.

title: D&D Head Dan Ayoub Opens Up on the OGL: “Trust Takes a Long Time to Build and a Second to Break”
content:
Three years after the OGL crisis, Wizards of the Coast is still working to win back the tabletop community — and the man running D&D says he knows the clock is ticking.

Dan Ayoub, who took over as Head of Dungeons & Dragons in 2025, spoke with Wargamer’s Mollie Russell about the fallout from the OGL, the lessons learned since, and the new direction he’s steering the brand toward.

A Candid Admission

Ayoub didn’t dance around the subject when asked where Wizards went wrong with the OGL. He said the company lost sight of who D&D actually belongs to.

“It was a rug pull, right?” Ayoub told Wargamer. “A lot of people and businesses were built up around a specific thing. Trust was given to the brand, and people rightly felt the rug was pulled from under them.”

He also pointed to a broader mistake: assuming there’s a one-size-fits-all way to play D&D. Ayoub said his job isn’t to tell players how to run their games — it’s to give them the tools to do it their way.

Rebuilding Trust Won’t Be Quick

Ayoub describes his first year in charge as a mix of rewarding and terrifying, and he’s under no illusions about how long it takes to repair damaged trust.

“My biggest takeaway as I step into this role is that trust takes a long time to build and a second to break,” he said. “I’m keenly aware it’s going to take me a long time to repair this.”

If he deserves credit for one thing so far, he says it’s listening. Wizards established a community council, and Ayoub has personally spent time talking with fans, retailers, and consumers.

The Fallout Reshaped Everything

The OGL controversy didn’t stay contained to Wizards — it sent ripples through the entire industry, from Creative Commons releases to Pathfinder moving away from OGL-based rules. Ayoub compared it to a cataclysmic event from D&D’s own lore.

“I’m a big Dragonlance fan, and it was kind of like when the mountain dropped and reshaped the geography,” he said. “It fundamentally changed the ecosystem and everything about it.”

Stepping into the role afterward wasn’t easy. Ayoub called it “fucking terrifying,” admitting he was worried about damaging something he’s loved his whole life. But that love is exactly why he took the job — he wants to get D&D back to how he remembers it.

Bringing Outside Voices Back In

A major part of the new direction is collaboration. Wizards has been reaching out to classic creators like Margaret Weis, Tracy Hickman, Bob Salvatore, and Luke Gygax, along with partners like Ghostfire Gaming, which is taking on Ravenloft. Ayoub said he doesn’t want Wizards to be the only voice for D&D.

“The voice of D&D was only coming from one place, but that’s not how D&D grows,” he said. “I want to bring more people in to tell more stories.”

He noted the irony of it all, given D&D’s most famous advice: “The fundamental mantra is don’t split the party, and we went ahead and split the party.”

The Community Group Is Already Making a Difference

The D&D Community Advisory Group, launched in June, has been giving Wizards direct — and blunt — feedback. Ayoub said one early note changed how the company operates: members told him Wizards was doing cool things but doing a terrible job telling people about them. That led directly to publicizing the roadmap.

The group has even scrapped product ideas before they reached players. Ayoub values having people who’ll tell him when something isn’t working.

Looking Ahead

Ayoub says he’s never going to stop listening, and he’s holding himself to the promises he made when he took the role. He’s also thinking long-term — someone will eventually sit in his chair and celebrate D&D’s 100th anniversary, and that only happens if the game keeps growing.

The full interview, which also covers D&D’s franchise model, the Netflix and HBO projects, and how Ayoub is opening doors for new designers, is available at Wargamer.

title: Steve Jackson Steps Down as CEO After 46 Years
content:
Steve Jackson is handing over the reins. The founder of Steve Jackson Games is stepping down as CEO after leading the company for 46 years, returning to what he’s always loved most: designing games.

Sabrina Gonzalez, a longtime SJG staffer, is taking over as CEO. Allison Page, previously Managing Editor, has been promoted to Chief Operating Officer.

The news was announced Friday, September 11, 2026, via press release and a follow-up post on the company’s blog, the Daily Illuminator. SJG is inviting fans to drop by their forums and congratulate both Gonzalez and Page on their new roles.

The End of an Era

Jackson founded SJG in 1980 after several years at Metagaming, and his fingerprints are all over the tabletop hobby. He created GURPS (Generic Universal Role Playing System) in 1983 — a genre-agnostic RPG now in its fourth edition, which Jackson and line editor Sean Punch have continually refined over the decades.

Other staples from his design career include the party favourite Munchkin, the quick-playing Zombie Dice, and the sci-fi wargame Ogre.

Jackson ran the company with an unusual degree of transparency, publishing yearly “report to stakeholders” blog posts. But SJG has struggled to keep pace with the wider industry in recent years — a challenge reflected in both its public-facing identity and its ability to pull in new customers. Modern players tend to gravitate toward either experimental indie titles or established giants like D&D and Pathfinder.

Jackson was always a designer first and a business owner out of necessity. Handing the CEO role to Gonzalez may give the company room to get back to what it does best.

Who Is Sabrina Gonzalez?

Gonzalez joined SJG in 2013 and has been with the company ever since, aside from a brief 2025 detour into game manufacturing that broadened her view of that side of the business. She’s held roles including Production Artist and Production Manager, and has sat on the company’s Board of Directors since 2021.

As for her goals, she’s thinking about both the future and the past. “As a general goal, I’d like us to continue to grow,” she said. “We weathered the pandemic and pivoted project plans to address continually changing tariffs. The goal is always to make great games that people love. I want to continue developing new titles for future generations of gamers and also support (and sometimes update) the classics that our fans continue to request.”

That dual approach is already taking shape. SJG recently struck a deal with Possum Creek Games to publish and sell its RPG catalogue, including Wanderhome and Yazeba’s Bed & Breakfast, bringing on Jay Dragon as lead game designer and Ruby Lavin as art director. The company has also licensed indie RPGs like Luke Jordan’s Grand Guignol and Caro Acersion’s Last Train to Bremen.

Away from the desk, Gonzalez is a fan of party and dice games — dominoes is her all-time favourite and travels with her. She’s also a multi-instrumentalist who plays guitar, piano, ukulele, and more.

One of her fondest SJG memories: one of her first assignments was designing everything for the Munchkin Tavern, from the logo to the signage and menus. A photo of the 2013 Tavern logo ended up on a T-shirt signed by many attendees that year — a memento that reminds her of good times with people who are no longer with us. “We still think of and miss you greatly, Andrew Hackard,” she said.

Who Is Allison Page?

Page joined SJG in 2023 as Managing Editor. Before that, she was Executive Artistic Director of Killing My Lobster, a San Francisco sketch comedy outfit, and worked as a Narrative Designer in video games — her entry point into the industry.

Like Gonzalez, Page gravitates toward party games. She describes herself as fiercely competitive and happy to take any excuse to shout and laugh. She’s been a comedy writer and playwright for over a decade, spending much of her time writing, reading others’ work in her writing group, and hanging out with fellow writers complaining about writing — which she considers a crucial part of the craft.

What’s Next for SJG

A few things are already in motion:

  • Steve Jackson will focus on game design and development. No specific projects have been announced yet.
  • Dragon’s 7 Part Pact — a complex RPG about wizards governing an archipelago through baroque politics and a shaky balance of occult power — recently raised over $1,000,000 from nearly 5,800 backers. Fulfillment and retail are currently estimated for late 2027.
  • Munchkin 5.5E RPG, designed in partnership with Lynnvander Studios, is expected to hit Backerkit next month.

Both Gonzalez and Page say they’re ready for the challenge and looking forward to ushering in a new era for the company.

title: D&D Delves Back Into the Underdark With New Playtest Options
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released a second round of Underdark-themed playtest material for Dungeons & Dragons, and it’s packed with new ways to build a character from the deep places of the world.

The new Unearthed Arcana: Underdark Options 2 PDF introduces three subclasses and five new species, all drawing on the strange, dangerous corners of D&D’s most storied subterranean setting. The survey opens on D&D Beyond starting September 17, so there’s time to test these options at your table before weighing in.

Three New Subclasses

The playtest features a mix of brand-new concepts and one returning favourite:

  • Freedom Domain (Cleric) — A high-Dexterity Cleric built around liberation, movement, and breaking chains. Its spell list was designed with a single question in mind: would this spell help in a jailbreak? Channel Divinity lets allies shake off conditions like Frightened, Grappled, Paralyzed, or Restrained and reposition without provoking opportunity attacks.
  • Circle of Spores (Druid) — An update to the subclass originally from Guildmaster’s Guide to Ravnica and Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, now tuned for 5.5e. The Underdark version leans harder into the myconid connection, granting Telepathy and reworking the old Spreading Spores feature into Explosive Burst — which makes your zombies detonate in a cloud of damaging spores when they die.
  • Faerzress Sorcery (Sorcerer) — Built around faerzress, the weird magical radiation of the Underdark. This Sorcerer can create zones of faerzress, ignore its drawbacks, and eventually transform into a being of pure faerzress energy. Lightning damage is the subclass’s signature flavour.

Five New Species

The species lineup is where things get really interesting. Rather than playing visitors from the surface, these options let you play characters who already call the Underdark home:

  • Deep Imaskari — Descendants of humans who fled into the depths millennia ago, now infused with the magic of “Unlight.” They create light rather than relying on Darkvision, and gain a versatile Aura of Unlight at level 3.
  • Drider — The classic drow-spider hybrid, finally playable. You get Spider Climb, Web Walker, and spells of the Spider Queen, with mechanics inspired by the Centaur from Mordenkainen Presents: Monsters of the Multiverse.
  • Illithidkin — Victims (or willing participants) of mind flayer experimentation. They get psionic abilities, Psychic resistance, and telepathy. Notably, this is a separate route from the Ceremorphosis feat path in the previous UA, not meant to be combined with it.
  • Kuo-toa — Fishlike humanoids with a talent for creating bizarre, sometimes living idols. Their Deific Manifestation feature lets you cast Find Familiar and mix and match traits from two different forms to build your own little abomination.
  • Myconid — Bipedal fungal folk and the ultimate team players. Their abilities focus on building rapport, sharing knowledge, and granting the whole party telepathy through spores.

What the Design Team Is Saying

Senior Game Designer Jason Tondro noted that this UA touches on elements of the Underdark that have appeared before but are being “expanded or transformed in ways we’re not yet ready to fully reveal.” Faerzress, for example, dates back to 1978’s D1 Descent into the Depths of the Earth, while the Deep Imaskari first appeared in 2003’s Underdark supplement.

The material uses the Player’s Handbook rules, and Wizards is clear that these options are experimental — they may end up more or less powerful than what’s currently in the game, and could change significantly before any official publication.

How to Get Involved

If you want to help shape what makes it into a future D&D book, now’s your chance. Try these subclasses and species in your campaign or a one-shot, then fill out the survey on D&D Beyond when it goes live on September 17.

Worth noting: the document includes a content warning for body horror and mind control, so keep that in mind depending on your table.

title: Discworld Returns to the Tabletop with New Modiphius RPG
content:
Modiphius Entertainment is heading back to the Disc — and this time it’s trading the cobbled streets of Ankh-Morpork for the hills, forests, and castles of the Ramtops.

The publisher has announced Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald, a brand-new tabletop RPG launching on Gamefound this October. It follows the success of Discworld: Adventures in Ankh Morpork, which raised over £2m on Kickstarter during its 2025 campaign.

A Standalone Trip to the Ramtops

The good news for newcomers: you won’t need the first book to jump in. Adventures in Lancre and Überwald is a standalone core rulebook, playable with or without its predecessor. That makes it an easy entry point for anyone who’s been curious about Discworld roleplaying but didn’t back the original campaign.

The new book explores three iconic corners of Terry Pratchett’s world:

  • Lancre — home turf of the witches
  • Überwald — the gloomy, vampire-heavy region beyond the mountains
  • The Chalk — the rural downland region introduced in the later Discworld novels

Play as Witches, Vampires, Trolls, and Werewolves

Players will be able to encounter — and play as — witches, vampires, trolls, and werewolves, opening up a much wider range of character options than before. The book also brings in plenty of fan-favourite characters and locations, from the Ogg clan to Don’tgonearthe Castle to Granny Weatherwax herself.

For the first time in the official Discworld RPG line, there are also full rules for running ongoing campaigns, plus a book of linked adventures that takes players on a tour of the Ramtops.

What’s in the Campaign

Modiphius is promising a hefty spread of options when the Gamefound campaign goes live in October, including:

  • A hardcover core rulebook in standard and collector’s editions
  • An adventure book
  • A GM Toolkit
  • Additional supplements
  • Dice

The publisher is also putting extra focus on onboarding. The book includes expanded guidance and support for new players and gamemasters, with more examples that lean into the humour and wit Pratchett’s series is known for. There are also expanded rules for complex challenges, new risks for taking multiple consequences, and plenty of common situations explained in full — all of which Modiphius is billing as the easiest entry point yet for newcomers to both Discworld and tabletop RPGs in general.

More Discworld on the Way

This isn’t the only Discworld project in Modiphius’s pipeline. The publisher also has Kill Sam Vimes, a light board game about pursuing the titular character, and Readers Digested, a licensed edition of Reiner Knizia’s Blue Moon City, both available to pre-order now.

The Discworld: Adventures in Lancre and Überwald Gamefound campaign launches in October.

title: Wizards of the Coast Releases Exodus TTRPG, Tying Into Upcoming Sci-Fi Video Game
content:
Wizards of the Coast has released Exodus, a new sci-fi tabletop RPG set in the same universe as the upcoming AAA video game from Archetype Entertainment. The Traveler’s Handbook and Exodus Encyclopedia are now available for purchase through the official Exodus webpage.

Designed by James Ohlen—the veteran RPG designer behind Baldur’s Gate 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic—the game adapts the 5E system for sci-fi play, with new classes, weapons, and factions. The Traveler’s Handbook introduces eight origins, four classes with two subclasses each, and six powerful Traveler Dynasties that serve as in-game factions. The Exodus Encyclopedia packs in stat blocks for constructs, Celestials, changelings, awakened beings, and human NPCs, along with Remnant items for research and combat.

Both books are full-color hardcovers with Smythe sewn binding and spot UV finishing. The project also features contributions from award-winning sci-fi authors Adrian Tchaikovsky and Peter F. Hamilton.

The Exodus video game is slated for release in 2026 on PC, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S.

title: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana Returns – Chaosium’s Definitive Mythos Guide Hits in October
content:
Chaosium is releasing a new fourth edition of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana this October, bringing the definitive guide to Lovecraftian horror back to shelves in full-color hardback format.

First published in 1994 and updated several times since, the book compiles detailed entries on mythos deities, creatures, tomes, and artifacts—from Azathoth to Zylac—tracing their appearances across fiction and pop culture. This new edition features updated text, evocative interior art, and a cover by John Sumrow, along with a fresh essay from author Dan Harms on the question “What is the Cthulhu Mythos?” Timelines of the Necronomicon, a cosmic horror bibliography, and illustrations of Nyarlathotep, Hastur, and Cthulhu himself round out the package.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana releases October 28—just in time to send a shiver down your spine before Halloween.

title: CMON Faces Make-or-Break Moment as It Warns of “Prolonged Structural Downturn”
content:
CMON has issued a stark warning about its future, telling investors its core business is stuck in a “prolonged structural downturn” and still burning through more cash than it brings in. The tabletop crowdfunding giant is now racing to raise up to $17.5m from outside investors.

The warning landed alongside CMON’s H1 financial report, and it caps off a brutal 18 months for one of the biggest names in crowdfunded board games.

Parts of this article is based on info from BoardGameWire.

A Company Half Its Former Size

CMON has spent the past year and a half trying to stop the bleeding. The publisher has:

  • Cut its workforce in half
  • Sold off major IP including Zombicide, Blood Rage, and Cthulhu: Death May Die
  • Shut down its Singapore office
  • Halted new crowdfunding campaigns

Those moves have helped — but not enough to fix the underlying problem.

Losses Shrinking, But Cash Still Draining

The good news: CMON’s losses are shrinking fast.

The company posted a loss of just over $2m in the first half of 2026, compared to nearly $7m during the same stretch last year. Revenue also crept up more than 7% year-on-year, hitting $3.68m. Selling and distribution costs were cut by more than half, and administrative expenses dropped from $4.37m to $2.37m.

The bad news: it’s still not enough to keep the lights on without outside help.

CMON’s cash reserves have been in freefall. They sat at $3.9m at the end of 2022, fell to $2.1m by the end of 2024, and slipped to just over $900,000 by June 2025. In early August, the company revealed it had roughly $368,000 on hand — less than a month’s worth of operating expenses.

The Backer Problem: $14m in Undelivered Games

A huge chunk of CMON’s financial pressure comes down to games that backers have already paid for but haven’t received.

Eight crowdfunded titles remain undelivered, representing $14m raised from backers. The two biggest are **DC Super Heroes United** (over $4.4m raised) and DCeased (over $2.5m). Both were originally due last year, but have been delayed repeatedly and are now slated for Q1 2027.

CMON hasn’t completed fulfillment on a crowdfunding project since Zombicide: White Death in mid-2025. It has managed to ship some pre-orders — Cthulhu: Dark Providence, Marvel United: Witching Hour, and Dune: Desert War all went out in the first half of this year — but four more pre-order titles remain in limbo, including the Assassin’s Creed Role Playing Game.

The $17.5m Gamble

To stay afloat, CMON is leaning on a massive rights issue designed to raise up to HK$150.5m (about $19m). The plan lets existing shareholders buy three new shares for every one they already own.

There’s just one problem: shareholders barely took the bait. Only 7.76% of the new shares were claimed by the August deadline, leaving CMON scrambling to find more than $17.5m from other investors — a figure approaching 2.5-times the company’s entire valuation from its last share sale in February.

If the money comes through, here’s how CMON plans to spend it:

  • 40% — Day-to-day operations for roughly a year, including staff, royalties, shipping, and distribution
  • 20% — Paying down debts, including $2.46m owed to a company director and $385,000 in unsecured employee advances
  • 25% — Expansion into existing and new markets, with a focus on Europe, Japan, and the Philippines
  • 15% — Potential acquisitions in digital gaming

The final result of the rights issue is due September 15.

A Digital Pivot — With a Catch

That 15% digital acquisition budget is notable, especially since CMON just walked away from a planned $2.1m investment in NFT game maker Blissful Link. That deal would have valued Blissful Link at over $95m — despite the company posting a loss of about $197,000 in 2024 on revenues of just over $408,000.

CMON says it’s now hunting for one to three businesses, mostly in Asia-Pacific, valued between $1.3m and $2.5m each, to help build digital adaptations and companion apps. The publisher insists physical tabletop games remain its core business and that digital is meant to complement, not replace, them.

Where the Money Comes From Now

The report also lays bare just how dramatically CMON’s geographic revenue has shifted.

North America generated over $8.6m in the first half of 2021 — 57% of the company’s roughly $15.1m revenue at the time. By the first half of 2026, North and South America combined brought in just $642,000.

Europe has collapsed similarly, falling from about $4.5m to $982,000 over the same period.

Asia is now CMON’s largest market by a wide margin, generating over $2m and accounting for about 55% of total revenue — up from less than 10% in 2021. That’s not because Asia is growing, though. Revenue there is down roughly 37% since 2022. It’s just fallen far less than everywhere else.

What’s Next for Crowdfunding?

CMON said back in March that it intended to resume crowdfunding in the second half of 2026. Its latest report doesn’t repeat that promise. Instead, the company says new titles will be developed and launched “selectively” based on market conditions, available cash, and project readiness.

For a publisher built on the crowdfunding model, that’s a notable shift in tone — and a sign that CMON’s road back to stability is still a long one.

title: This Monty Python-esque comedy RPG lets you improv as a band of incompetent and dangerously powerful wizards
content:
Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is a new tabletop roleplaying game that allows players to become powerful and incompetent spellcasters.

The upcoming roleplaying game sees any number of players collaborating together to tell a story about a band of chaotic wizards. Similarly to the likes of absurdist, fantastical comedy such as the works of iconic British group Monty Python, alongside the likes of The Mighty Boosh and What We Do in the Shadows, Hello Wizard I have a Problem is all about rapid scenes infused by the strange and unexpected.

Unlike many other tabletop RPGs, Hello Wizard sees its players taking turns to take on the roles of player character and games master. Each scene in Hello Wizard has a single player take the spotlight as their spellcaster, with the goal of impressing their fellow sorcerers with their magic. The active player describes what spells their wizard casts, with the other players acting collectively as a GM and deciding how these spells can go wrong.

Players will use a Problem Generator included in the fantasy RPG’s rulebook as inspiration for what could go wrong with the wizards’ spells, with the book capable of making over “200,000” prompts for possible disastrous outcomes. Once every player has had the opportunity to step into the spellcasting spotlight at least a few times, the game ends and players tally up their ‘points’ - which are decided by a loose improv system - and determine who is the most impressive wizard.

The rules system for Hello Wizard is very straightforward and intended to be easy for players to learn. Setup for the tabletop RPG is also designed to be quick and easy, with players expected to start in little time. The rulebook for the game will contain advice and optional rules players can use to augment their playthroughs too.

Hello Wizard I have a Problem was created by Sam Armstrong, a tabletop RPG designer who has previously made titles such as All Bastard - a fantasy TRPG in which players take the roles of either a band of bragging heroes or the bastards they defeated - and horror roleplaying game Slasher. The artwork for the game was created by illustrator Evlyn Moreau, who has previously worked on RPGs like Liminal High School.

The crowdfunding campaign for Hello Wizard I Have a Problem is on Kickstarter until later this afternoon, with the title potentially being made available on Armstrong’s Itch.io page. A pledge of £8 ($10) will get backers a physical copy of the game in June, alternatively a PDF version is available for £4 ($5).

title: Re-enact Greta Gerwig’s Little Women with this coming-of-age tabletop RPG
content:
New tabletop roleplaying game, Castles in the Air, will enable players to re-enact their favourite coming-of-age stories.

Castles in the Air was inspired by the likes of classic coming-of-age period dramas such as Little Women by Louisa May Alcott - which was adapted into a 2019 film directed by Greta Gerwig and starring Saoirse Ronan, Emma Watson, Florence Pugh, Laura Dern and Timothee Chalamet - and Anne of Green Gables by Lucy Maud Montgomery, which was adapted into a televisions series in 2017 by Netflix.

The upcoming roleplaying game will see players’ characters grow up together from children to adults during the historical era known as the Gilded Age, which took place in the USA from the 1870s to the 1890s and saw an increase in industrialisation, economic growth and migration to the US. Castles in the Air is a collaborative storytelling game in which players construct narratives that centre around the wonders and fears of childhood, before tackling the joys and hardships of adulthood.

Players begin the tabletop RPG as a tight-knit group of children, all of whom have great expectations of their futures and much quieter current lives. In this phase of the story, players develop a shared childhood together by doing the things rural and financially supported kids did during that era: like playing in their local farmlands, swimming in the lakes and watching the stars.

As the player characters grow up, they’ll begin exploring other feelings and ideas that come with age. Characters in the group might develop a crush on someone or form a heated rivalry with one of the other local children. All the while, the player group will grow up together, before eventually reaching adulthood and potentially finding themselves drifting apart as life takes them in different directions - perhaps to only meet once again.

Players will be able to create their characters in Castles in the Air by choosing from a variety of character roles inspired by classic archetypes, such as the troublesome scamp, studious bookworm or spoiled princess. Add onto this a dream, childhood relationships, a family background and a bosom enemy, and players can even create their favourite characters from the likes of Little Women or Anne of Green Gables.

Castles in the Air was designed and written by Melia Carraway, with contributions from co-created by the co-founders of the RPG’s publisher, Storybrewer’s Roleplaying, Vee Hendro and Hayley Gordon, who also co-designed Good Society: a tabletop RPG inspired by the works of Jane Austen.

The crowdfunding campaign for Castles in the Air is on Kickstarter until June 9th, with a pledge of AU$ 99 (£52/$77) getting backers a physical copy of the game in March 2025. Alternatively, players can get a digital version for a pledge of AU$ 34 (£18/$26).

title: Freak War throws Exploding Kittens and Pokémon into a blender for a trading card game you can play at parties
content:
Take the evolving monsters of Pokémon, cross them with the fast-playing chaos of party game hit Exploding Kittens and you end up with something that looks a lot like Freak War, a new party-game TCG that wants to offer the fun battles of trading card games without the effort of learning lots of rules or building a deck.

Freak War is the creation of Nate Galbraith, aka cartoonist sketchnate, who was inspired after watching kids trying to have Pokémon battles using Uno cards, before suggesting they play classic playing card game War (which you might also know as Battle) instead. The result was a mixture of all three, with Galbraith adding a collection of strange creatures to the cards.

Unlike the head-to-head battles of Pokémon, Freak War can be played with up to four (or more) players, who can simply split the shuffled deck between them to play - though there is the option to build your own custom decks if you really want to.

Everyone plays a creature at the same time, with the highest attack level winning the battle. Like Exploding Kittens, the many cards can also introduce various effects that shake things up, including the power to evolve into bigger creatures - Pokémon-style - and equip modifiers to your own or opponent’s cards to boost or reduce their strength.

Whether the players choose a card from their hand or simply flip the top of their deck depends on the mode they’re playing: the more chaotic War, or the more strategic Battle. Both modes can be modified further by King of the Hill and team rules.

If two players draw in attack level, they both discard a card before facing off by playing another creature. The overall winner takes all the cards played and adds them to their win pile, which are reshuffled into the player’s deck - the person who manages to claim all the cards from their opponents, wins.

The weird and wonderful creatures on the cards have a bit of lore behind them, having been created by the emergence of a second sun that mutated familiar animals like rabbits, foxes and fish into muscly fishpeople, a time-travelling tiger, a partying platypus, a dog with a goldfish bowl for a head, a sad bee and a Man Cat that appears to basically be a bloke in a cat costume, among others.

Modifier cards, meanwhile, range from a Super Sword (and a Super Duper Sword) to the power to swap cards with a rival, cancel a modifier or flip coins for the chance of a power boost. Some of the creature effects get playfully meta in the way you’d expect for a party game too, with the scrap-loving Fly Guy gaining power if there’s uneaten food near the players.

As someone who is admittedly tired of many copy-paste or just downright gross party games (looking at you, double-offending Cards Against Humanity clones), I’m fairly charmed by Galbraith’s goofy creations and the sprinkling of chaotic take-that gameplay in the form of a TCG. (The card layout is quite explicitly inspired by Pokémon cards.) Sure, it’s not going to be for everyone, but as something knowingly silly to fill five minutes with friends and family (especially younger players), it looks like solid, breezy fun for $20 a deck. With a bunch of different packs filled with dozens more creatures from buff penguins to cute-looking snails, I’m pretty intrigued just to see Galbraith’s interpretation of the nonsense of modern Pokémon evolutions, too.

Freak War has already passed its fairly modest crowdfunding goal of $10,000 over on Kickstarter, where its campaign will run until June 13th. The game itself is expected to land with backers next June, just in time to take on holiday.

title: New Blade Runner RPG expansion asks how far you’d go for the Replicant Rebellion
content:
A new expansion for the official Blade Runner tabletop roleplaying game invites you to join the Replicant Rebellion.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game is based on the series of films based on Phillip K Dick’s sci-fi novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep.

Blade Runner, the first of these films, was released in 1982 and directed by Ridley Scott. The film sees Harrison Ford play Deckard, a Blade Runner - an officer whose sole purpose is to hunt and eliminate Replicants, or human-looking androids - who is tasked with finding and killing three escaped Replicants. Following on from the original film, Blade Runner 2049 is a sequel directed by Denis Villeneuve and starring Ryan Gosling. In Blade Runner 2049, Gosling stars as K, a Replicant Blade Runner who must follow the trail of a long-escaped Replicant fugitive and investigate the truth behind her death.

Both films take place in the same fictional science fiction universe wherein Replicants were designed and created entirely to fulfil the needs and wants of their human makers. The Blade Runner franchise is known for its cyberpunk aesthetics, as well as grim view of a near-future wherein corporations are able to commit terrible acts without consequence and exploit large swathes of people.

Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game usually has players taking the roles of Blade Runners within the LA police department during the time period between the first and second films. However, rather than fulfilling their duties as Replicant hunting officers, the next expansion for the sci-fi RPG sees players abandoning their post to join the Replicant Underground.

Replicant Rebellion is a new expansion for the Blade Runner RPG that sees players get recruited into the Replicant Underground, a secret organisation whose goal is to ensure the freedom and liberation of Replicants: whatever the cost.

Players will see themselves become members of the movement - running their own independent crew as they carry out a variety of missions on behalf of the Underground. From laying charges for explosives, sabotaging the Replicant trade and smoking out moles, players must be prepared for all manner of tasks. Members of the group might even find themselves stuck between a rock and a hard place, as they balance their personal morality with the operations of the Replicant Underground.

Both the Replicant Rebellion expansion and the Blade Runner roleplaying game were published and created by Free League Publishing, the studio behind other licensed TRPGs such as the Alien Roleplaying Game.

A crowdfunding campaign for Blade Runner: The Roleplaying Game - Replicant Rebellion will be launched on Kickstarter on May 28th.

title: City of Six Moons is a board game written in an alien language you’ll need to translate to play - and you’ll never know if you’ve got it quite right
content:
Upcoming board game City of Six Moons is taking difficulty-to-decipher rulebooks to a whole new level by writing all of its rules in an alien language that you’ll have to translate in order to play. The kicker? You’ll never know if you’ve done so correctly.

The single-player title is described by designer Amabel Holland as being both a game about guiding the fortunes of an alien civilisation, and a game designed as if it actually were made by an alien civilisation in real life.

As such, Holland has written the entire rulebook in a language composed of icons, glyphs and symbols, setting a challenge to the player to decipher the language before they can read the rules for the game itself. To work out its secrets, you’ll apparently need to draw on both your own existing cultural assumptions and the acceptance that the culture of the alien civilisation who made it is very different to humanity.

Cheekily, Holland proposes that players will never quite know if they’ve perfectly cracked the code, and she will refuse to answer any questions about the game’s rules. (Well spotted, BoardGameGeek.)

Given all that, we obviously don’t quite know how the game will play, or even how long it'll take to finish, only that it’ll be a solitaire experience with a set of components needed to play the game in the box alongside the rulebook. Presumably those components will either be devoid of language or marked in the same code as the rules, though we also don’t know what game pieces will be included just yet. We have seen the cover artwork at least, which presumably might offer a first clue to decoding the iconographic language.

Holland did confirm over on Bluesky that City of Six Moons will be a “functional, replayable game” for those who do successfully figure out its rules (or enough to play, that is), though deciphering the code is considered a key part of the package - meaning that players might find it a “lesser” experience after they know its secrets. Yet even that permanent change in understanding is part of the overall journey, Holland believes: “That loss is a thing I want you to feel; I want it to linger.”

City of Six Moons is due for release next month from Holland’s own (alongside co-owner Mary Holland) publishing label Hollandspiele. Good luck to anyone preparing to tackle the cryptic puzzle.

title: Alternate cover for Dungeons & Dragons’ Player’s Handbook radiates a wholesome vibe for players who want to D&D and chill
content:
The front cover for the alternate version of the next Dungeons & Dragons Player Handbook has been revealed.

Last week saw the unveiling of the artwork for the front cover of the Player’s Handbook, for the next version of tabletop roleplaying game - Dungeons & Dragons. Featuring depictions of classic characters from the history of the RPG - such as Strongheart the Knight, Elkhorn the Dwarf Warrior and Yolande the Elven Queen - the front cover shows a party of D&D adventurers and heroes preparing to fight against a horde of Kobolds, a classic Dungeons & Dragons enemy, with a friendly golden dragon standing behind them.

The artwork strongly implies that the group is in the midst of a battle, thereby emphasising the action elements of the fantasy roleplaying game over anything else - which is what D&D is largely known for, at least amongst the general public.

By contrast, the artwork for the front cover of the alternate version of the new D&D Player’s Handbook was revealed soon afterwards - showing a much different approach. (Thanks Polygon) Designed for collectors or players who aren’t keen on the appearance of the standard version, the alternative versions of D&D books don’t differ much from their standard counterparts beyond the outside aesthetics and front cover.

The artwork for the cover of the alternate version of the next D&D Player’s Handbook also depicts a party of adventurers, this time in a very different situation from those shown on the front of the standard book. A classic Dungeons & Dragons party - complete with wizard, cleric, fighter and rogue - are shown sharing a pot of tea inside what looks like the inside of a cave. Included within this serene tea party is a golden dragon - somewhat linking things back to the standard cover - who grasps a normal-sized tea cup in one massive paw, with the party’s rogue balancing on part of the dragon’s body above.

This illustration by artist Wylie Beckert, who is also responsible for the front cover of the alternative version of Dungeon & Dragons: Tasha’s Cauldron of Everything, certainly gives off a very different vibe to that of the cover for the standard version of the new Player’s Handbook, which was created by Tyler Jacobsen, providing players who prefer a more relaxed and introspective approach to roleplaying with a more suitable option.

The alternate version of the new D&D Player’s Handbook will be available from local game stores from September 3rd, before the wider release of the book on September 17th.

title: Spend another five hours moving three spaces in the new Talisman board game from the studio behind Betrayal at House on the Hill
content:
A new edition of Talisman, the classic adventure board game, is coming from the publisher behind Betrayal at House on the Hill.

Originally released in 1983, Talisman is a board game wherein two to six players compete to acquire the Crown of Command, which is held directly in the centre of the board. The original edition of the title was published by Games Workshop - the company behind the Warhammer and Warhammer 40K series of miniatures games - and designed by Robert Harris. In the game, players choose from a selection of characters inspired by classic fantasy roleplaying game archetypes, before travelling through each ring of the board in order to reach the middle.

The series has changed over the years, with Fantasy Flight Games - the company behind the recent Star Wars Unlimited trading card game - taking over publishing rights in 2008 before releasing a revised version of the Fourth Edition of the title. As players progress through the game, they’ll acquire new equipment, abilities and allies they can use to overcome the various challenges that block them from entering the inner rings of the board. Gaining these advantages can require players to pass a skill check of some kind, with each starting character offering a different array of statistics.

Players may also have to defeat a rogue’s gallery of monsters during the fantasy board game, all for the goal of completing a Talisman quest in order to enter the board’s inner world. Other players may challenge each other through combat, with any losing player being forced to fall back behind the winner. Whichever player reaches the Portal of Power first claims the Crown of Command, which they can use to eliminate all other players and win.

Talisman 5th edition, officially known as Talisman: The Magical Quest Board Game - 5th Edition, will be published by Avalon Hill, a studio that’s best known for releasing the horror board game series Betrayal at House on the Hill. The upcoming board game will have players competing for the iconic Crown of Command by making their way through the board’s rings towards the middle space. Players will be able to choose from 12 different playable characters: including a thief, a monk, a warrior, a ghoul and a sorceress.

This new edition will feature 100 different adventure cards for players to encounter during their journey through the land of Talisman, all of which include illustrations - with the entire board game containing brand new artwork and updated components. The gameplay for 5th edition has been “streamlined” to make it more accessible to less experienced players, with no more details about its gameplay available beyond that.

Talisman: The Magical Quest Board Game - 5th Edition is set to be released on August 1st for a retail price of $60 (£47).

title: Hannibal and Hamilcar bring two out-of-print classic historical wargames back to crowdfunding (Sponsored)
content:
This article is sponsored by Phalanx. Find out more about Hannibal & Hamilcar and back it on Gamefound until May 24th.

Two classic historical board games retelling the clash between Rome and Carthage during the Punic Wars have returned to crowdfunding, giving you another chance to pick up the out-of-print pair of card-driven strategy titles.

The latest Gamefound campaign for Hannibal & Hamilcar brings together designer Mark Simonitch’s acclaimed nineties wargame Hannibal: Rome vs. Carthage, in its new streamlined and revised Classic Edition, with Hamilcar: Silver Edition, designed by Raymond de Maria based on Simonitch and John Rodriguez’s Hannibal companion game Hamilcar: First Punic War, which used similar gameplay mechanics and some of the same components to focus on the naval portion of the conflict.

Both games put a card-driven system at their heart, with each of two players controlling either Rome or Carthage using an asymmetrical deck of strategy cards to command their units around the map, reinforce their armies, sway different regions to their control and trigger historical events based on the period. When armies collide - whether on land or at sea - a separate set of battle cards are used to resolve clashes, requiring players to juggle their political and military ambitions to achieve overall victory.

Hannibal & Hamilcar’s combined re-release in 2018 was named BoardGameGeek’s Best Wargame at the Golden Geeks that year, with the original Hannibal: Rome vs. Carthage taking home the same award and the top prize for Best 2-Player Board Game a decade earlier. The two-in-one title currently sits at a BoardGameGeek user rating of 8.3 out of 10, with over 6,700 reviews, making it the 18th highest-rated wargame on the site at the time of writing. Unlike the collected re-release of Hannibal & Hamilcar, this latest printing sees the two games' newest editions offered as separate boxes.

Publisher Phalanx’s latest crowdfunding campaign for Hannibal & Hamilcar over on Gamefound provides another chance to pick up the out-of-print games - separately, or together in a bundle - along with a new exclusive set of metal miniatures finished in a dark wash to represent the Roman and Carthaginian generals in both titles. The miniatures will only ever be available via the crowdfunder, Phalanx confirmed.

Both games can be had for €80 together or €45 each, with the 26 metal miniatures contained in a €95 wooden storage box illustrated with Hannibal Barca; €160 will get you the full package of both games and the new shiny figures. The re-released games are expected to arrive in August next year, with the Gamefound campaign giving you until May 24th to pledge.

title: This new eBay rival for TCGs wants to make buying and selling ungraded Pokémon cards less of a headache
content:
Speaking from experience, buying and selling rare Pokémon cards on the internet can be a bit of a nightmare. Outside of the cards pricey enough to be officially graded and sealed inside a fancy case by the likes of PSA, looking for less top-dollar cards (look, I’m not Post Malone) comes with the constant risk of stumping up the cash for something that either doesn’t arrive at all, arrives in a condition different to what you were expecting or turns out to be a complete fake.

I’m therefore intrigued by the lofty promises being made by new TCG marketplace startup Ungraded, founded by a couple of Cornish Pokémon card collectors (that is, the collectors are Cornish - they're not collecting Pokémon called Pastyrnip or something) who reckon they’ve come up with a way of trading cards for real money without the fuss and frustration of rolling the dice online.

As the name suggests, Ungraded plans to focus on ‘raw’ cards for the likes of Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh!, as well as other trading cards like those for football or American sports, that haven’t yet been given an official rating of their condition.

Rather than requiring sellers to send their cards off to a separate specialist and pay to get them graded or - on the opposite end of the spectrum - end up listed with a couple of blurry photos on something like eBay, Ungraded's seemingly unique imaging technology will snap enough high-resolution photos of cards submitted by sellers to create a 3D preview for potential buyers to peruse.

The apparent promise is that the company’s “groundbreaking” 3D technology is accurate enough to let customers properly judge a card’s condition by rotating and zooming in on the digital replica formed by hundreds of ultra high-definition photos - even being able to view things like CMYK print patterns, as well as any scuffs, scratches or centring - meaning they can be seemingly assured of its condition before placing a bid, even without seeing it in person.

It’ll be free for sellers to sell cards worth over £25, with buyers paying a fee equal to 20% of the card’s sold value for those worth up to £250; more expensive cards will then lower the rate to 17.5% for cards up to £1,000 and 15% for the most pricey cards over a grand. Cards listed with a fixed price won’t have an extra buyer fee attached - sellers will instead pay 15% - and cards worth under £25 will charge the seller the difference between 20% of the card’s value (paid by the buyer) and the £5 minimum fee.

As cards listed for sale are sent off to Ungraded to be snapped and uploaded, any cards that aren’t sold after 30 days will be charged an unsold fee worth 1% of the card’s average price every 30 days after that - so best hope your card goes quickly. When they are sold, Ungraded says it’ll cover costs like postage and insurance - so sellers should just have to send their cards in.

Ungraded plans to launch its marketplace this July, running a series of auction drops from the end of May that will include Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh! and Magic: The Gathering cards. It sounds fairly ambitious, as these things do, so it'll be interesting to see how it fares come the summer.
